one: Relational databases store tables with a fixed schema and joins. "NoSQL" is a grab-bag: document, key-value, wide-column and graph stores, each optimised for one access pattern.
an: A relational DB is a well-organised filing cabinet with cross-references. A key-value store is a coat check: hand over a ticket, get one coat back, extremely fast, nothing else.
how: Relational (PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server): tables, foreign keys, joins, transactions, a flexible query language. Postgres also does JSON, full-text search and geospatial (PostGIS).

Document (MongoDB, Firestore): JSON-like documents, flexible shape, data read together is stored together. Key-value (Redis, DynamoDB): lookup by key, very fast. Wide-column (Cassandra, ScyllaDB): huge write volumes across many nodes. Graph (Neo4j): relationships are first-class (social graphs, fraud rings).
The real question is your access patterns: what you query, how often, and what must stay consistent.
why: Picking a store that fights your access pattern is one of the most expensive mistakes to undo. Seniors are expected to justify the choice.
trade: The pragmatic default for most products is Postgres, adding specialised stores (Redis for cache, a search engine, an analytics warehouse) when a concrete need shows up.

myth.m: NoSQL scales and SQL does not.
myth.r: Postgres runs huge products. NoSQL stores scale writes horizontally more easily by giving up joins and some consistency. That trade only pays off at specific scales and shapes.

q.s: A marketplace with orders, payments, refunds and inventory that must never go negative. Default database choice?
o: A relational DB like Postgres, for transactions and constraints
Redis only
A graph DB
Cassandra
q.e: Money and stock need ACID transactions and constraints. You can add Redis for caching later.

more: Data modeling by access pattern (single-table design in DynamoDB)
Postgres JSONB: when a document column inside SQL is enough
Time-series databases (TimescaleDB, InfluxDB)
Analytical (OLAP) columnar stores: ClickHouse, BigQuery, DuckDB
Polyglot persistence and its operational cost
lab: Model the same blog (users, posts, comments, tags) in Postgres tables and in MongoDB documents. Write the 3 most common queries in each.
Store a flexible "settings" object in a Postgres JSONB column, index one key with a GIN or expression index, and query it.
Try DuckDB on a CSV file to feel what a columnar analytics engine is like.

plain:
A relational (SQL) database stores data in tables with fixed columns and connects tables with IDs. It is great at keeping data correct and answering flexible questions.

“NoSQL” is a name for many different databases that each specialise in one way of storing data: whole JSON documents, simple key-value lookups, huge write volumes, or relationships between things. The right choice depends on how you will read and write the data.
bridge: If you have used Firebase or Supabase, you have seen both sides: Firestore is a document (NoSQL) database; Supabase is PostgreSQL (SQL). The trade-offs you felt there are exactly this topic.

walk.title: Choosing a database for a car-wash booking app
steps: Data: users, venues, time slots, bookings, payments, monthly payouts.
Key rules: a slot must never be double-booked; money records must never be half-written.
Those rules need transactions and constraints, which relational databases do best. Choose PostgreSQL.
Venues need “find near me” search. Postgres with PostGIS handles that, so no second database yet.
Later, if real-time counters get heavy, add Redis next to Postgres for that one job, not instead of it.

terms: Tables, rows, columns, joins; e.g. PostgreSQL, MySQL.
Stores JSON-like documents; e.g. MongoDB, Firestore.
Get and set by key, very fast; e.g. Redis, DynamoDB.
The defined structure of your data.
Which questions you ask the data, and how often.
insights: Default to Postgres unless you can name the specific need it does not meet.
“NoSQL scales better” is mostly a myth at normal scale; it scales differently, by giving up joins and some guarantees.
Most mature products use several stores, each for what it is good at, with one clear source of truth.

prod.summary: In production the question is rarely “SQL or NoSQL” but “which store is the source of truth, and which extra stores do we accept the operational cost of”. Seniors start from the access patterns (the 5–10 queries that carry the product), the consistency rules (money, stock, bookings) and the team's ability to run the thing at 3 a.m.
checklist: Write down the top access patterns with expected rates (reads/s, writes/s) and latency targets before naming a database.
List the invariants that must never break (no double booking, balance never negative). If they span several records, you need multi-row transactions and constraints.
For a document or key-value store, check the item size limit and design around it (MongoDB 16 MB per document, DynamoDB 400 KB per item).
For DynamoDB or Cassandra, design the partition key first: every hot query must hit one partition, and no single key may get most of the traffic.
Check if Postgres features already cover the need: JSONB + GIN for flexible fields, PostGIS for geo, full-text search, pgvector for embeddings.
For every extra store, name the owner, the backup/restore plan and how it is kept in sync with the source of truth.
Confirm analytics will not run on the primary OLTP database; heavy reports belong on a replica or a warehouse.
numbers: MongoDB maximum BSON document size is 16 MB.
DynamoDB maximum item size is 400 KB; one partition serves up to 3,000 read units and 1,000 write units per second.
PostgreSQL default max_connections is 100, so “just add another service talking to Postgres” has a real ceiling.
failures: DynamoDB returns ProvisionedThroughputExceededException / throttling on one key even though table capacity looks fine.

A hot partition: one partition key (one tenant, one “global” counter) gets most traffic, and each partition has its own limit. Fix the key design: spread writes with a suffix (write sharding), or move the counter elsewhere.
A MongoDB write fails with “BSONObjectTooLarge” after months in production.
An array inside one document grew without limit (all comments embedded in a post). Store unbounded lists as separate documents/collections and reference them.
Totals in the NoSQL store disagree with the payments table; support finds orders that were “paid twice”.
Two stores were written separately without a transaction or outbox, and one write failed. Keep money in one transactional store; feed other stores from it via an outbox or CDC (change data capture).
The team added Redis, Elasticsearch and MongoDB in year one; on-call pages are mostly about sync bugs and version upgrades.
Polyglot persistence without a concrete need. Consolidate onto Postgres where its features are enough, and keep extra stores only where you can name the query they serve.

code.title: Document-style data inside Postgres with JSONB
code.note: Strict columns (price, sku) keep constraints; only truly variable fields go in attrs. jsonb_path_ops supports @> and is smaller than the default GIN operator class.

qs.s: An IoT product ingests 200,000 sensor readings per second across 5 regions. Queries are always “readings for device X between t1 and t2”. No joins, no cross-device transactions. Which design fits best?
o: A single Postgres primary with one table and a B-tree on (device_id, ts)
A wide-column store (Cassandra/ScyllaDB) with partition key device_id plus a time bucket, clustering by ts
MongoDB with one document per device holding all readings in an array
Neo4j, because devices are connected
qs.e: The access pattern is one key plus a time range at very high write volume across regions, which is exactly what wide-column stores are built for. One document per device would hit the 16 MB limit. A single Postgres primary is a write bottleneck at this rate (Postgres with partitioning/Timescale can work at lower volume).

qs.s: A team wants MongoDB “because the schema changes often”. Their data: users, teams, invoices, invoice lines, payments, with reports joining all of them. What is the strongest counter-argument?
o: MongoDB cannot store nested data
MongoDB has no indexes
The data is relational with cross-entity reports and money rules; Postgres migrations plus a JSONB column handle schema change without giving up joins and constraints
NoSQL databases cannot run in the cloud
qs.e: Schema flexibility is a weak reason when the data is heavily related and needs consistency. Migrations are routine, and JSONB covers the genuinely flexible parts. The other options are simply false.

qs.s: You store a shopping cart per user, read and written only by user_id, and losing a cart after a crash is acceptable. Postgres is already the main DB. What is the most reasonable choice?
o: Keep carts in Postgres for now; move them to Redis/DynamoDB only if cart traffic becomes a measured problem
Add Cassandra immediately
Build a graph database model of carts
Store carts in the search engine
qs.e: A key-value store fits the shape, but adding a system has a permanent cost. At normal scale a Postgres table keyed by user_id is fine; switch when metrics show the need. That is the senior default: specialise on evidence.

qs.s: A team designs a DynamoDB table for orders. The “open orders” screen queries PK = "STATUS#open". At peak, writes are throttled although the table's total capacity is far from used. Why?

code.title: item

o: Every open order shares one partition key, so all writes hit one partition and its per-partition limit (about 1,000 write units/s); spread the key (e.g. STATUS#open#<0-9>) or use a sparse GSI
DynamoDB does not allow # in keys
The sort key is too long
On-demand mode cannot handle peaks
qs.e: Capacity is spread across partitions, but each partition has its own limit. A low-cardinality key like a status puts all traffic on one. Write sharding (a suffix) or a sparse index spreads it. Even on-demand tables are limited per partition, so switching mode does not fix a hot key.

qs.s: An architect says: “We cannot use MongoDB for orders and payments, because MongoDB has no transactions.” What is the accurate answer?
o: Correct: MongoDB only has single-document atomicity
Wrong: MongoDB has supported multi-document ACID transactions since 4.0 (replica sets) and 4.2 (sharded clusters); the real questions are the data model, their cost, and the team's experience
Correct, unless you use Atlas
Wrong: MongoDB wraps every query in a transaction by default
qs.e: Single-document writes are atomic, and multi-document transactions exist, with time and performance limits. The better argument is about fit: heavily related data with cross-entity reports and money rules is usually easier in a relational model. Repeating an old myth in a design review weakens a good argument.

qs.s: Read this Cassandra error. What is the right fix?

code.title: cqlsh
code.src:
cqlsh> SELECT * FROM readings WHERE temperature > 30;
InvalidRequest: Error from server: code=2200 [Invalid query]
message="Cannot execute this query as it might involve data
filtering and thus may have unpredictable performance. If you want
to execute this query despite the performance unpredictability,
use ALLOW FILTERING"

-- table: PRIMARY KEY ((device_id, day), ts)

o: Add ALLOW FILTERING
Add a secondary index on temperature and keep the query
Increase the read timeout
Model the query: create a table whose partition key matches it (for example alerts by day with a temperature bucket), written at ingest time; or run this as an analytics job (e.g. Spark)
qs.e: In Cassandra you design one table per query, keyed by what you look up. This query has no partition key, so it would scan every node. ALLOW FILTERING makes it run, with exactly that full-cluster cost. Secondary indexes on high-cardinality, range-queried columns perform badly in Cassandra.

qs.s: Product wants a dashboard: revenue by country by day over 3 years (500M order rows). On the Postgres OLTP primary the query takes 4 minutes and slows checkout. Best direction?
o: Add more indexes on orders
Move orders to MongoDB
Feed a columnar analytics store (ClickHouse, BigQuery, DuckDB on exports) via CDC or batch, or at least use a pre-aggregated daily table on a replica
Run the query with a higher work_mem on the primary
qs.e: Aggregations over hundreds of millions of rows read only a few columns; columnar stores read just those columns and compress well, so they are often 10–100× faster. Indexes do not help much when most rows are read. Moving to a document store makes analytics harder, not easier.

interview.q: How would you choose the database for a new product?
answer: Start from access patterns (the 5–10 queries that carry the product), their rates and latency targets.
List the invariants: money, stock, bookings. Multi-row rules need transactions and constraints.
Default to a relational database (Postgres) unless a named need does not fit: extreme write volume across regions, a key-value shape at huge scale, graph traversals.
Check what Postgres already covers: JSONB, full-text search, PostGIS, pgvector, partitioning.
Consider operations: who runs it, backups, upgrades, the team's experience, managed options and cost.
Add specialised stores later for one job each, fed from one source of truth.
followups: What would make you pick DynamoDB from day one?
How do you migrate if the choice turns out wrong?

interview.q: How does data modelling in DynamoDB differ from Postgres?
answer: Postgres: model the entities and relationships, then write any query; indexes and the planner adapt.
DynamoDB: list the access patterns first; design partition and sort keys (and GSIs) so each is a single Query on one partition.
Joins do not exist; related items are stored together (single-table design) or duplicated.
New access patterns later may need a new GSI or a backfill, which is harder than adding an index in Postgres.
Limits shape the design: 400 KB per item, per-partition throughput, eventually consistent reads by default.
followups: How do you avoid a hot partition?
How do transactions work in DynamoDB?

interview.q: Postgres JSONB: where is it a good idea and where does it stop being one?
answer: Good for truly variable fields (per-category product attributes, webhook payloads, settings), with GIN indexes for containment queries.
Keep fields with rules as real columns: money, foreign keys, status, anything with constraints or frequent filtering.
Limits: no foreign keys inside JSON, weaker statistics for the planner, updating one key rewrites the whole value.
Very large JSON values are stored out of line (TOAST), which makes reads and updates expensive.
If every query reads the same JSON keys, they probably should be columns.
followups: How would you index a single JSON key used in ORDER BY?
How do you migrate a JSON key into a real column?

videos.why: Seven database paradigms and what each is good at.

videos.t: How To Choose The Right Database?
videos.why: A practical way to choose a database for a project.

one: A separate sorted data structure that lets the database find rows without scanning the whole table.
an: The index at the back of a textbook. Without it you read all 900 pages to find "mitochondria"; with it you jump to page 412.
how: The default is a B-tree: a balanced sorted tree. Lookups, range queries (>, BETWEEN) and ORDER BY on indexed columns become logarithmic instead of linear.

Composite indexes on (user_id, created_at) help queries filtering by user_id, or by user_id and created_at. Column order matters (leftmost prefix rule). Postgres 18 added skip scan, which can use the index for created_at alone, but only works well when user_id has very few distinct values, so do not design around it.
Read the plan with EXPLAIN ANALYZE: "Seq Scan" on a large table in a hot query is the red flag; "Index Scan" or "Index Only Scan" is what you want.
why: Missing indexes are the most common cause of slow apps. A query going from 2s to 2ms with one index is a routine senior fix.
trade: Every index slows writes (it must be updated on every insert/update) and takes disk. Functions on columns (WHERE lower(email) = ...) skip a plain index unless you create an expression index. Low-selectivity columns (a boolean) rarely benefit.

myth.r: Writes get slower, storage grows, and separate single-column indexes are weaker than one well-ordered composite index (Postgres can combine them with a bitmap scan, but that is usually slower). Index for your real queries.

q.s: Query: WHERE status = 'paid' AND created_at > now() - interval '7 days'. You have an index on (created_at, status). Better index?
o: (status, created_at): equality column first, range column last
An index on status only
No index
Two separate single-column indexes always beat one composite
q.e: Put equality filters first and the range filter last, so the B-tree can seek to status='paid' and scan only the recent range.

more: Index-only scans and covering indexes (INCLUDE)
Partial indexes (WHERE deleted_at IS NULL)
GIN (JSONB, arrays, full-text), GiST (geo, ranges), BRIN (huge append-only tables)
Selectivity, statistics and why the planner ignores an index
Finding unused and duplicate indexes
lab: Create a table with 1M rows. Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a filter query: note Seq Scan and time.
Add an index, re-run, compare plan and time.
Build a composite index in the wrong column order, see it not used for one query, then fix the order.
Create a partial index for active rows only and compare its size (\di+).

plain:
Without an index, the database finds rows by reading the whole table, row by row. With an index, it uses a sorted lookup structure to jump straight to the matching rows.

The right index can make a query 1,000 times faster. But every index also slows down inserts and updates a little, because it must be updated too.
bridge: It is like a Map vs array.find() in JavaScript: find checks every item, a Map jumps to the key. An index is a Map the database keeps for you.

walk.title: Fixing a slow “my orders” page
steps: Query: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20. It takes 1.8 seconds.
Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on it. The plan says “Seq Scan on orders”, reading all 3 million rows.
Create CREATE INDEX ON orders (user_id, created_at DESC).
Run EXPLAIN again: “Index Scan”. The DB jumps to user 42's orders, already sorted by date, and reads only 20 rows.
Time drops to 2ms. Order of columns matters: (user_id, created_at) helps this query; (created_at, user_id) would not.

terms: A separate sorted structure for finding rows quickly.
The default index type: a balanced sorted tree.
Reading the whole table. Fine for small tables, bad for big ones in hot queries.
Shows how the database ran a query and how long each step took.
An index on several columns, in a specific order.
insights: Check the query plan before adding a cache or a bigger server. A missing index is the most common cause of a slow endpoint.
Unused indexes are not free insurance: each one slows every insert and update and adds vacuum work. Remove them.
The plan that matters is the production one. Stale statistics or a different data distribution can make the planner skip an index that works in staging.

prod.summary: In production, indexes are driven by the slow-query log and pg_stat_statements, not by guessing. Seniors check that every hot query has a matching index, that new indexes are built without blocking writes, and that unused indexes are removed, because each one costs write speed, disk and vacuum time.
checklist: Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on the real query with production-like data; check estimated vs actual rows and look for “Rows Removed by Filter” in the thousands.
Order composite index columns: equality filters first, then range or sort column (e.g. (tenant_id, status, created_at)).
Build indexes on live tables with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, and check afterwards that it is not left INVALID.
Use partial indexes for the common filter (WHERE deleted_at IS NULL) and expression indexes for lower(email).
Every foreign key column used in joins or ON DELETE CASCADE has its own index; Postgres does not create it automatically.
Check pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan = 0 over weeks to find unused indexes, and drop duplicates.
After a big data load, run ANALYZE so the planner has fresh statistics.
numbers: A Postgres index can have at most 32 columns (including INCLUDE columns).
A B-tree entry is limited to about 2,704 bytes with the default 8 KB page; longer values fail with “index row size … exceeds btree version 4 maximum 2704”.
Postgres creates indexes automatically for PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE constraints, but not for foreign key columns.
failures: Deleting one customer takes 40 seconds and locks things up.
The orders.customer_id foreign key has no index, so each cascade or FK check does a sequential scan of orders. Add an index on the FK column (concurrently).
A query uses the index in staging but does a Seq Scan in production.

Different data distribution or stale statistics: the planner estimates the filter matches a large share of rows. Run ANALYZE, compare estimated vs actual rows, and consider a partial or more selective composite index.
WHERE lower(email) = $1 is slow even though email is indexed.
A function on the column cannot use a plain index. Create CREATE INDEX ... ON users (lower(email)) or use the citext type.
After a failed CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, inserts get slower but the query is still slow.
The build failed and left an INVALID index: it is updated on every write but never used for reads. Find it with \d table (marked INVALID), drop it, and rebuild.
Insert throughput dropped 30% after a “performance” sprint.
Many new indexes, each updated on every insert. Check idx_scan and drop the ones queries do not use.

code.title: Reading a plan before and after the right index
code.src:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, total_cents FROM orders
WHERE tenant_id = 7 AND status = 'paid'
ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;

-- Before: Limit -> Sort -> Seq Scan on orders
--   Filter: ((tenant_id = 7) AND (status = 'paid'::text))
--   Rows Removed by Filter: 2841733      <- the red flag

CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_tenant_status_created
  ON orders (tenant_id, status, created_at DESC)
  INCLUDE (id, total_cents);             -- every selected column

-- After (once VACUUM has set the visibility map):
-- Limit -> Index Only Scan using orders_tenant_status_created
--   Index Cond: ((tenant_id = 7) AND (status = 'paid'::text))
--   Heap Fetches: 0                      <- no Sort, no table reads

-- Find indexes nobody uses
SELECT relname, indexrelname, idx_scan
FROM pg_stat_user_indexes ORDER BY idx_scan ASC LIMIT 10;
code.note: Equality columns first, the sort column last, and INCLUDE for every other selected column, id too. Leave one out and the plan becomes a plain Index Scan that reads the table. Heap Fetches stays above 0 until VACUUM has marked the pages all-visible.

qs.s: Query: SELECT * FROM events WHERE user_id = $1 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50. Indexes exist on (user_id) and on (created_at). The plan sorts 80,000 rows for a heavy user. Best fix?
o: Increase work_mem so the sort is faster
Cache the page in Redis
Add an index on (created_at, user_id)
Replace them with one index on (user_id, created_at DESC)
qs.e: With (user_id, created_at) Postgres jumps to the user and reads rows already in order, stopping after 50. (created_at, user_id) puts the range/sort column first and cannot seek by user. More work_mem only makes the wasteful sort a bit faster.

qs.s: A tasks table has 50M rows; 99% have done = true. The worker polls WHERE done = false ORDER BY id LIMIT 100. What index is best?
o: CREATE INDEX ON tasks (done)
No index; booleans never benefit
CREATE INDEX ON tasks (id, done)
CREATE INDEX ON tasks (id) WHERE done = false
qs.e: A partial index contains only the ~500k pending rows, stays small, and is already ordered by id. A full index on a boolean is huge and does not give the order. “Booleans never benefit” is wrong when the value you query is rare.

qs.s: pg_stat_user_indexes shows orders_status_idx with idx_scan = 0 over 30 days, on a write-heavy table. A teammate wants to keep it “just in case”. What is the senior call?
o: Keep it; indexes are free
Check that stats were not reset and that no replica or monthly job uses it, then drop it concurrently
Rebuild it with REINDEX so it starts being used
Convert it to a hash index
qs.e: An unused index costs write speed, disk and vacuum work. Before dropping, confirm the statistics cover the period and check replicas (each has its own stats) and rare jobs. DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY avoids blocking.

qs.s: Read the plan. The query filters by tenant_id and status. What is the best fix?

code.title: EXPLAIN ANALYZE
code.src:
Index Scan using orders_tenant_id_idx on orders
    (cost=0.56..48210.11 rows=310 width=64)
    (actual time=0.04..412.77 rows=18 loops=1)
  Index Cond: (tenant_id = 42)
  Filter: (status = 'failed'::text)
  Rows Removed by Filter: 121482
Planning Time: 0.2 ms
Execution Time: 412.9 ms

o: Create an index on (tenant_id, status) (or a partial index ON orders (tenant_id) WHERE status = 'failed') so the index finds the 18 rows directly
Nothing; an Index Scan is always the best plan
Run VACUUM FULL on orders
Increase work_mem
qs.e: The index finds all 121,500 rows of tenant 42, then throws away all but 18 after reading them from the table. “Rows Removed by Filter” in the thousands is the signal. Seeing “Index Scan” makes people think the query is fine; what matters is how many rows were read to return how few.

qs.s: There is a B-tree index on orders(created_at). This query still does a Seq Scan on 40M rows. Which rewrite lets it use the index?

code.title: daily-report.sql

o: WHERE date(created_at) = '2026-10-01'
Add ORDER BY created_at
WHERE created_at >= '2026-10-01' AND created_at < '2026-10-02'
Cast the literal instead: WHERE created_at = '2026-10-01'::date
qs.e: A function or cast on the column hides it from a plain index. A half-open range on the raw column can use the B-tree. date(created_at) is the same function in another form. Comparing to a date literal changes the meaning (it matches only midnight). For timestamptz, also be clear which time zone defines “the day”.

qs.s: Inserts into a 300M-row events table slowed down over months. The primary key is uuid DEFAULT gen_random_uuid() (UUIDv4). The disk is fine and the PK index is much larger than the RAM cache. What is the main cause?
o: UUIDs are 16 bytes, so each insert writes too much data
Postgres cannot index uuid columns efficiently
The table needs to be partitioned by uuid
Random UUIDs land on random pages of the B-tree, so almost every insert reads and dirties a page not in cache; a time-ordered key (UUIDv7 or bigint identity) appends to the right edge of the index
qs.e: With sequential keys, new entries go to the same few “hot” pages at the end of the index, which stay in memory. Random keys touch pages all over a huge index, causing cache misses, more WAL (full-page writes) and page splits. The 16-byte size matters a little, but locality is the main problem. Postgres 18 has a built-in uuidv7().

qs.s: A database uses the en_US.UTF-8 collation. CREATE INDEX ON users (email) exists, but WHERE email LIKE 'kim%' does a Seq Scan. Why?
o: LIKE can never use an index
With a non-C collation, a default B-tree cannot be used for LIKE prefix searches; create the index with text_pattern_ops (or use the C collation for that column)
The planner statistics are stale; run ANALYZE
The index must be a hash index for string matching
qs.e: A B-tree sorted by language rules does not guarantee that all strings starting with “kim” are next to each other in a way LIKE can use. An index with text_pattern_ops compares byte by byte, so prefix matches become a range scan. LIKE with a leading % needs a trigram GIN index instead.

interview.q: A query is slow in production but fast on your laptop. Walk me through how you diagnose it.
answer: Find it with data: pg_stat_statements sorted by total time (calls × mean), or the slow-query log, not by guessing.
Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) with real parameters on production-like data (a replica or a restored snapshot).
Compare estimated vs actual rows; a big gap means stale or poor statistics (ANALYZE, extended statistics).
Look for Seq Scans on large tables, big “Rows Removed by Filter”, sorts spilling to disk, nested loops with many loops.
Check for the non-index reasons too: lock waits (pg_stat_activity.wait_event), N+1 patterns, or a cold cache.
Fix with the smallest change (composite, partial or expression index, or a query rewrite), build it CONCURRENTLY, and re-measure.
followups: The plan is different for one tenant than for others. Why can that happen?
When would you NOT add an index even though it speeds up the query?

interview.q: How do you decide the column order in a composite index?
answer: Columns compared with equality go first, then the range or ORDER BY column, so the B-tree can seek to one place and read a contiguous slice.
Match the sort direction of the main query (e.g. created_at DESC) so LIMIT can stop early without a sort.
The leftmost prefix rule: (a, b, c) serves filters on a, a+b, a+b+c; not b alone (Postgres 18 skip scan helps only when a has few distinct values).
Among equality columns, order matters less for that query; pick an order that also serves other queries.
Add INCLUDE columns for index-only scans when the selected columns are few.
followups: Would you add (a, b) if (a) already exists?
How does a partial index compare with adding the column to the index?

interview.q: You need to add an index to a 500M-row table that takes 2,000 writes per second. How do you do it safely?
answer: Use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY: it does not block writes, but it is slower, does two table scans and cannot run in a transaction.
Set a lock_timeout; even CONCURRENTLY waits for older transactions to finish, so kill or wait out long-running ones first.
Check disk space for the new index and the extra WAL; watch replica lag during the build.
If it fails, it leaves an INVALID index that still slows writes: find it, drop it, retry.
Measure afterwards: the target query uses it, and write latency did not get worse.
On partitioned tables, build on each partition concurrently, then attach to an index created with ON ONLY the parent.
followups: Why does CONCURRENTLY wait for unrelated transactions?
How do you find indexes you can drop?

diagrams.title: Seq Scan vs Index Scan for “my orders”

one: A transaction groups several writes so they all happen or none do. ACID names the guarantees.
an: A bank transfer: money must leave account A and arrive in B together. Half a transfer is worse than none.
how: Atomicity: all or nothing (BEGIN ... COMMIT, or ROLLBACK on error). Consistency: constraints (foreign keys, unique, check) hold after commit. Isolation: concurrent transactions do not see each other's half-done work (to a configurable degree). Durability: once committed, it survives a crash (written to the write-ahead log).
Constraints are part of the deal: a UNIQUE index stops two signups with the same email even when your app code races.
Keep transactions short. Never call a slow external API (payment provider, email) while holding a transaction open.
why: Without transactions, a crash between two writes leaves corrupt data: an order with no items, stock decremented with no order.
trade: Long transactions hold locks and block others. Transactions do not span services, which is why distributed systems need sagas and the outbox pattern.

myth.m: My app checks for duplicates before inserting, so I do not need a unique constraint.
myth.r: Two requests can both check, both see nothing, both insert. Only the database constraint is race-proof.

q.s: Checkout: (1) create order, (2) decrement stock, (3) call payment API, (4) mark paid. What belongs inside one DB transaction?
o: All four, including the payment call
Steps 1 and 2; call payment outside, then update the order in a second short transaction
None
Only step 3
q.e: A network call inside a transaction holds locks for seconds and cannot be rolled back anyway. Keep the DB work atomic and handle the external call as a separate step with its own failure handling.

Write a transfer function that debits and credits two accounts inside a transaction; throw an error between the two updates and confirm nothing changed.

plain:
A transaction groups several changes into one unit: either all of them happen, or none do. If anything fails in the middle, the database undoes the partial changes.

ACID is the name for the guarantees: all-or-nothing, rules always respected, concurrent work does not see half-finished changes, and committed data survives crashes.
bridge: Think of a React state update that must change three pieces of state together. If only one changed, the UI would be inconsistent. A transaction gives you that “together” guarantee for data that matters.

walk.title: Moving money between two accounts
steps: BEGIN;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id = 'A';
The server crashes right here, before the second update.
Because the transaction was never committed, the database rolls back the first update on restart. A still has its 100.
On a normal run: the second update adds 100 to B, then COMMIT; makes both changes permanent at the same instant.

terms: A group of changes that succeed or fail together.
Undo all changes in the transaction.
A rule the DB enforces, like UNIQUE or CHECK (balance >= 0).
insights: Most transaction bugs are not in the SQL but in the code around it: two pooled connections instead of one, no ROLLBACK in a catch, or an await on a slow API in the middle.
A constraint only helps users if its error is handled: map SQLSTATE 23505 to a clear 409, not a 500.
When a flow touches a payment provider or another service, decide up front which side is the source of truth and how you reconcile when they disagree.

prod.summary: In production, transactions are about two things: correctness (constraints and all-or-nothing writes for money, stock and bookings) and keeping them short, because an open transaction holds locks and stops vacuum from cleaning up. Seniors look for network calls inside transactions, missing constraints, and connections left “idle in transaction”.
checklist: Every business rule that must never break is a constraint (UNIQUE, CHECK, FOREIGN KEY, NOT NULL), not only app code.
No HTTP calls, emails, queue publishes or file uploads between BEGIN and COMMIT.
The transaction uses one client from the pool for all statements, and the client is released in finally.
Set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout (and on Postgres 17+ transaction_timeout) so a stuck request cannot hold locks forever.
Unique-violation errors (SQLSTATE 23505) are mapped to a clear 409/422 response, not a 500.
Events that other systems need are written to an outbox table in the same transaction, not published directly.
Monitor the oldest open transaction: SELECT max(now() - xact_start) FROM pg_stat_activity.
numbers: Postgres idle_in_transaction_session_timeout, statement_timeout and lock_timeout all default to 0 (disabled).
transaction_timeout was added in PostgreSQL 17; it also defaults to 0.
SQLSTATE 23505 = unique_violation, 23503 = foreign_key_violation, 23514 = check_violation.
failures: pg_stat_activity shows sessions in state “idle in transaction” for minutes; other queries wait on locks; table bloat grows.

Code opened a transaction, then awaited a slow external call or crashed without rollback. Move external calls outside, always ROLLBACK in a catch, and set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout (e.g. 60s).
Orders exist with zero items after a deploy that “refactored the repository layer”.
The two inserts now run on different pooled connections (pool.query twice), so they are not in one transaction. Use one client: pool.connect(), BEGIN, both inserts, COMMIT.
Customers report two accounts with the same email.
Uniqueness was checked in app code only; two concurrent signups both passed the check. Add a UNIQUE index on lower(email) (after cleaning duplicates) and handle error 23505.
Payment was charged at the provider but the order is still “pending” in the DB.

The process crashed between the external call and the second transaction. Use an idempotency key with the provider and a reconciliation job or webhook that marks the order paid; a DB transaction cannot cover an external system.

code.title: A correct transaction with node-postgres
code.note: Using pool.query for each statement would send them to different connections, and BEGIN/COMMIT would not cover them. The ROLLBACK guard keeps the original error and stops a broken connection from going back into the pool. Call the payment API after COMMIT; the outbox row is published by a separate worker.

qs.s: Code: await pool.query('BEGIN'); await pool.query('INSERT INTO orders ...'); await pool.query('INSERT INTO order_items ...'); await pool.query('COMMIT'); with a pool of 10. Under load, some orders have no items. Why?
o: Postgres does not support multi-statement transactions
The pool is too small
Each pool.query may use a different connection, so the statements are not in the same transaction
COMMIT should come before the inserts
qs.e: A transaction belongs to one connection. pool.query picks any free connection each time, so BEGIN might run on connection 1 and the inserts on 2 and 3, autocommitting separately. Use pool.connect() and one client.

qs.s: A nightly job runs BEGIN; UPDATE ... 2 million rows ...; COMMIT; and takes 25 minutes. During it, the app's writes to the same table time out. What is the best change?
o: Process in batches of a few thousand rows, each in its own short transaction
Raise statement_timeout for the app
Run the job at Serializable isolation
Wrap the job in two nested transactions
qs.e: One giant transaction holds row locks on everything it touched until COMMIT and blocks vacuum. Small batches release locks quickly. Higher timeouts only hide the waiting; Serializable adds conflicts.

qs.s: Signup flow: insert user, then send a welcome email via an API, all inside one transaction. The email API sometimes takes 10 seconds. What problems does this cause? Pick the most complete answer.
o: None, because the email is sent before COMMIT
Only that emails are slow
The connection and any locks are held for 10s, so the pool drains under load; and if COMMIT later fails, the email was already sent for a user who does not exist
The database will reject the transaction for being too long
qs.e: External calls inside a transaction cause pool exhaustion and inconsistency, because an email cannot be rolled back. Commit first, then send (ideally via an outbox job). Postgres has no default transaction time limit, so it will not reject it.

qs.s: This Prisma code is meant to be atomic. Under load, product stock goes down for orders that were never saved. Find the bug.

code.title: checkout.ts

o: Interactive transactions need isolationLevel: "Serializable"
decrement is not atomic
The stock update uses prisma instead of tx, so it runs on another connection outside the transaction and commits (or fails) independently
The outbox write should be outside the transaction
qs.e: Only queries made through tx belong to the transaction. The global client takes another pooled connection and commits at once. If a later step fails or the transaction times out, the order rolls back but the decrement stays. Under load it gets worse: each transaction holds one connection and waits for a second one, so transactions hit the 5 s interactive timeout. decrement is an atomic stock = stock - n in SQL, so it is not the problem. The outbox write must be inside: that is the whole point of the pattern.

qs.s: Read this session. Why do the last statements fail, and what should the code have done?

code.title: psql

o: After any error, Postgres marks the whole transaction as failed; every command is rejected and COMMIT becomes ROLLBACK. Use INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, or a SAVEPOINT before the risky statement and ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT on error
audit_log has a broken foreign key
The connection was lost after the first error
COMMIT should have been sent before the second insert
qs.e: Unlike some databases, Postgres does not let a transaction continue after an error. Apps that catch the unique violation in code and keep using the same transaction hit exactly this. Note that COMMIT reported ROLLBACK: nothing was saved, including the audit row.

qs.s: To speed up writes, a service sets synchronous_commit = off (wal_writer_delay is at its default of 200 ms). The server loses power. What can happen?
o: The database is corrupted and must be restored from backup
Nothing; committed data is always safe
Some uncommitted transactions become visible
Transactions committed in roughly the last 600 ms (up to 3 × wal_writer_delay) may be lost, although clients were told they succeeded; the database stays consistent
qs.e: With synchronous commit off, Postgres reports success before the WAL is flushed to disk. A crash can lose the most recent commits, but it cannot corrupt data or apply half a transaction. It is a durability trade-off you can even make per transaction (SET LOCAL) for low-value writes like analytics events.

qs.s: After the order transaction commits, the code publishes order.created to Kafka. Once a week an order is never shipped: the warehouse never got the event. What is the robust fix?
o: Publish to Kafka before COMMIT
Write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction as the order; a relay publishes outbox rows and marks them sent, and consumers are idempotent
Retry the Kafka publish 3 times
Use Serializable isolation
qs.e: The process can crash between COMMIT and the publish, so the event is lost. Publishing before COMMIT has the opposite bug: an event for an order that rolled back. The outbox makes “order saved” and “event recorded” one atomic write. The relay delivers at least once, so consumers must ignore duplicates. Retries do not help if the process died.

interview.q: Explain ACID with a concrete example. Which property is most often misunderstood?
answer: Example: a transfer debits A and credits B in one transaction.
Atomicity: both happen or neither, even if the server crashes in the middle (undone on recovery).
Consistency: constraints hold after commit (balance >= 0, valid foreign keys); it is only as good as the constraints you define.
Isolation: concurrent transactions do not interfere, to the level you choose; Read Committed still allows lost updates.
Durability: after COMMIT returns, the change is in the WAL on disk and survives a crash (unless you turn off synchronous_commit).
Most misunderstood: isolation. “It is in a transaction” does not make read-check-write safe.

What does the C in ACID mean compared with the C in CAP?

interview.q: A checkout flow writes to your database and charges a payment provider. How do you keep them consistent?
answer: A DB transaction cannot include the provider, so design for partial failure.
Create the order as pending in a short transaction, with an idempotency key.
Call the provider outside any transaction, passing the idempotency key so retries do not charge twice.
Mark paid in a second short transaction; also accept the provider's webhook, which handles the case where your process crashed after charging.
A reconciliation job compares pending orders with the provider and fixes either side; side effects (emails, events) go through an outbox.
followups: What happens if the webhook arrives before your own call returns?
When would you use a saga with compensation?

interview.q: What problems do long-running transactions cause in Postgres?
answer: Row locks are held until COMMIT, so other writers wait and request latency grows.
They hold back the cleanup horizon: VACUUM cannot remove dead rows newer than the oldest open snapshot, so tables and indexes bloat.
DDL like ALTER TABLE queues behind them and then blocks all traffic behind itself.
Pooled connections stay busy (“idle in transaction”), draining the pool.
Fixes: keep transactions short, no network calls inside, batch big updates, set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout and transaction_timeout (Postgres 17+), and alert on the oldest xact_start.
followups: How do you find the session that is blocking others?
Does a long read-only query on a replica affect the primary?

one: How much concurrent transactions are shielded from each other. Weaker levels are faster but allow specific anomalies.
an: Two cashiers selling the last concert ticket at the same second. Isolation decides whether both succeed.
how: Anomalies: dirty read (see uncommitted data), non-repeatable read (same row, different value within one transaction), phantom (new rows appear), lost update (two read-modify-writes, one overwrites the other), write skew (two transactions read the same data and each writes a different row, breaking a rule together).

SQL standard levels: Read Uncommitted → Read Committed (Postgres default) → Repeatable Read (MySQL InnoDB default) → Serializable (as if run one at a time; may abort transactions you must retry). In Postgres, Read Uncommitted behaves like Read Committed, and Repeatable Read also prevents phantoms.
Practical tools: atomic updates (UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE id = 1 AND qty > 0), SELECT ... FOR UPDATE row locks, or optimistic locking with a version column.
why: Overselling, double-booking and negative balances are isolation bugs. They only appear under real concurrency, so tests on a laptop rarely catch them.
trade: Serializable is simplest to reason about but needs retry logic. Row locks can deadlock if two transactions lock rows in different orders.

myth.m: Reading the value, checking it in code, then writing it back is safe inside a transaction.
myth.r: At Read Committed it is a classic lost update. Use an atomic UPDATE with a condition, a row lock, or a version check.

q.s: Two users book the last seat. Code: SELECT seats_left; if > 0 then UPDATE seats_left = seats_left_read - 1. Both bookings succeed. Smallest correct fix?
o: Add a cache
UPDATE ... SET seats_left = seats_left - 1 WHERE id = ? AND seats_left > 0, and check rows affected
Retry on failure
Use a CDN
q.e: The check and the write become one atomic statement. If zero rows were affected, the seat is gone.

Write skew (two doctors both going off call) and why Serializable catches it
Deadlock detection and consistent lock ordering
Advisory locks for app-level mutual exclusion
SKIP LOCKED for job queues in SQL
lab: Reproduce a lost update: two sessions read a counter, both write read+1. See one increment vanish.
Fix it three ways: atomic UPDATE ... SET n = n + 1, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, and a version column.
Set SERIALIZABLE in both sessions, reproduce write skew, and see one transaction fail with a serialization error you must retry.
Create a deadlock on purpose by locking two rows in opposite orders.

plain:
Many users change data at the same time. Isolation decides how much they can see of each other's unfinished work, and which conflicts the database prevents for you.

The classic bug: two requests both read “1 seat left”, both decide to book, both write. Now you sold the seat twice. Isolation levels, locks or atomic updates prevent this.
bridge: It is like two browser tabs editing the same document and both pressing save: the last save silently overwrites the first. Databases face that problem with thousands of “tabs” at once.

walk.title: The double-booking bug and its fix
steps: Request A: SELECT seats_left FROM events WHERE id = 1 → 1.
Request B, at the same moment, runs the same query → also 1.
Both see “1 > 0”, both run UPDATE events SET seats_left = 0 and both create a ticket. Two tickets, one seat.
Fix: one atomic statement: UPDATE events SET seats_left = seats_left - 1 WHERE id = 1 AND seats_left > 0.
The database runs these one at a time for that row. The first changes 1 row; the second changes 0 rows, so the app knows it is sold out.

terms: A bug where the result depends on timing between concurrent operations.
Two read-then-write operations where one overwrites the other.
Locks selected rows until your transaction ends.
A version number column; the update fails if someone changed the row since you read it.
The strictest level: as if transactions ran one after another.
insights: Ask of every write on money, stock or seats: “what if two of these run in the same millisecond?” If the answer depends on code between a SELECT and an UPDATE, it is a bug.
Defaults differ: code that was safe on MySQL (Repeatable Read) can behave differently on Postgres (Read Committed), and the other way round.
Serializable without a retry loop just turns silent races into 500 errors. Write the retry first.

prod.summary: In production, isolation bugs show up as oversold stock, double bookings and balances that do not add up, usually only under peak traffic. Seniors find every “read, decide in code, write” path on important data and make it safe with an atomic statement, a row lock, a version check or Serializable plus retries, and they make sure the retry logic exists before raising the isolation level.
checklist: List every read-modify-write on money, stock, seats and quotas; each one uses a conditional atomic UPDATE, FOR UPDATE, or a version column.
Code using Repeatable Read or Serializable retries the whole transaction on SQLSTATE 40001 (serialization_failure), with a small limit and jitter.
Deadlocks (SQLSTATE 40P01) are retried, and rows are locked in a consistent order (e.g. sorted by id).
Job queues in SQL use FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED so workers do not block each other.
Load tests include a concurrency test: 50 parallel requests buying the last item must produce exactly one success.
Know your database's default: Postgres is Read Committed, MySQL InnoDB is Repeatable Read; code moved between them can change behaviour.
Watch pg_stat_database.deadlocks and the rate of 40001 errors; a sudden rise means a new contention hot spot.
numbers: Postgres default isolation: Read Committed. MySQL InnoDB default: Repeatable Read.
Serialization failures always use SQLSTATE 40001; deadlocks use 40P01.
Postgres deadlock_timeout defaults to 1s: how long a lock wait lasts before the deadlock check runs.
failures: Flash sale: 1,000 units in stock, 1,047 orders confirmed.

Stock was read with SELECT, checked in code, then written back (lost update at Read Committed). Use UPDATE ... SET stock = stock - $1 WHERE id = $2 AND stock >= $1 and treat rowCount 0 as sold out; a CHECK (stock >= 0) constraint is a last safety net.
Logs show ERROR: deadlock detected on a transfer endpoint, a few times per hour.
Two transfers lock accounts A then B, and B then A. Lock both rows in id order (SELECT ... WHERE id = ANY($1) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE) and retry on 40P01.
After switching to Serializable, 2% of checkout requests return 500 with “could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions”.
Serializable aborts conflicting transactions by design. Wrap the transaction in a retry loop on 40001 (3–5 attempts with jitter). Without retries, Serializable just turns races into errors.
Two on-call doctors both went off call; the rule “at least one on call” is broken, with no error.

Write skew: each transaction read “2 on call” and updated a different row. Row locks on one row do not help. Use Serializable with retries, or lock the shared rows with FOR UPDATE on the whole on-call set.

code.title: Serializable transaction with retry on 40001 / 40P01
code.note: The whole function is re-run, including the reads, because the decision was made on data that is now stale. Keep fn free of side effects like emails. A conflict can surface on any statement or on COMMIT, so the catch covers both. The sleep sits after release(), so retries do not hold pool connections.

qs.s: A wallet service does SELECT balance ... FOR UPDATE, checks balance >= amount in code, then UPDATE balance = balance - amount, all in one transaction at Read Committed. Is it safe against double spending?
o: Yes: FOR UPDATE makes a second transaction wait until the first commits, then it reads the new balance
No: Read Committed always allows lost updates
No: you must use Serializable for any money
Yes, but only with a unique index on balance
qs.e: FOR UPDATE locks the row; a concurrent transaction blocks on the same SELECT FOR UPDATE and then sees the committed value. That prevents the lost update. Serializable would also work but is not required here.

qs.s: On Postgres, transaction A at Repeatable Read updates row 5. Transaction B, also Repeatable Read and started earlier, then tries to update row 5 after A commits. What happens to B?
o: B overwrites A's change silently
B fails with “could not serialize access due to concurrent update” and must retry
B waits forever
B's update is merged with A's
qs.e: Postgres Repeatable Read refuses to modify a row changed by a transaction that committed after B's snapshot. It raises a serialization error (40001). This is why code at Repeatable Read needs retries too.

qs.s: Ten worker processes each run SELECT * FROM jobs WHERE status = 'queued' ORDER BY id LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE. Throughput barely improves beyond one worker. Why, and fix?
o: Missing index on status; add it
Workers should use Serializable
Use a bigger connection pool
All workers try to lock the same first row and wait on each other; add SKIP LOCKED so each takes the next free row
qs.e: Every worker picks the same oldest job and blocks on its lock. FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED makes each worker skip locked rows and take a different one. An index helps speed but not the blocking.

qs.s: This code uses optimistic locking. Two requests update the same account at the same time. What happens?

code.title: wallet.ts

o: The second UPDATE blocks forever
Both succeed and the balance is decremented twice correctly
Postgres raises a serialization error for the second one
The second UPDATE matches 0 rows, but the code ignores rowCount, so it returns ok while its change was never applied
qs.e: The version check works in SQL: after the first update bumps the version, the second matches no row. But optimistic locking only helps if the app checks rowCount === 0 and then retries or reports a conflict. Here the user is told the payment succeeded. No error is raised at Read Committed; a zero-row UPDATE is not an error.

qs.s: Rule: at least one doctor must be on call. Alice and Bob are both on call. Both sessions run at REPEATABLE READ in Postgres, interleaved as shown. What is the result?

code.title: two sessions

o: B fails with a serialization error because it read data A changed
Both commit and no doctor is on call: write skew. Repeatable Read does not prevent it; Serializable would abort one of them
B waits on A's row lock, then sees count 1 and stops
A deadlock is detected and one rolls back
qs.e: Each transaction updates a different row, so there is no row conflict and no lock wait. Each decided based on a snapshot that the other one made false. Postgres Serializable (SSI) tracks these read/write dependencies and aborts one with 40001. Locking only your own row does not help; that is why this anomaly surprises people.

qs.s: A meeting-room booking service must never allow two bookings for the same room with overlapping times. Requests arrive concurrently. Which approach is both race-proof and simplest to keep correct?
o: An exclusion constraint: EXCLUDE USING gist (room_id WITH =, during WITH &&) on a tstzrange column (needs the btree_gist extension), and map the violation to HTTP 409
Check for overlaps with a SELECT, then INSERT, in one transaction at Read Committed
A UNIQUE index on (room_id, start_time)
Cache current bookings in Redis and check there first
qs.e: The database rejects any overlapping row no matter how requests interleave, just as UNIQUE does for equal values. SELECT-then-INSERT races at Read Committed: both see no overlap and both insert. A unique index on the start time only blocks identical starts, not 10:00–11:00 vs 10:30–11:30.

qs.s: A finance report runs at the default Read Committed: query 1 sums all balances, query 2 counts accounts by type. Transfers run during the report, and finance says the two numbers do not reconcile. Best fix?
o: Lock the accounts table during the report
Run the report on the primary instead of a replica
Use Serializable for every transfer
Run both queries in one REPEATABLE READ READ ONLY transaction, so they read the same snapshot
qs.e: At Read Committed each statement takes a new snapshot, so the two queries see different moments. Repeatable Read in Postgres gives the whole transaction one snapshot, and read-only transactions do not block writers. Locking the table stops all transfers for the report's duration, which is a much bigger cost.

interview.q: Explain lost update and write skew. How do you prevent each in Postgres?
answer: Lost update: two transactions read the same row, compute, and write; one write silently replaces the other. Example: two increments of a counter, one lost.
Prevent it with an atomic statement (SET n = n + 1, conditional WHERE stock >= $1), SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, or a version column with a rowCount check.
Write skew: two transactions read an overlapping set, then each writes a different row, and together they break a rule (the on-call doctors).
Row locks on your own row do not stop write skew. Use Serializable with retries, lock the whole set you read (FOR UPDATE on all rows), or materialize the conflict in one row or constraint.
Postgres Repeatable Read blocks lost updates on the same row (it errors with 40001) but allows write skew; Serializable prevents both.
followups: Why does Read Committed allow lost updates but not dirty reads?
How would you test for these bugs before production?

interview.q: Pessimistic vs optimistic locking: when would you use each?
answer: Pessimistic (FOR UPDATE): lock before deciding. Good when conflicts are frequent (hot rows like stock of a popular item) and the transaction is short.
Optimistic (version column): no lock while the user thinks; check at write time. Good for low-conflict data and long user edits (a form open for minutes).
Pessimistic risks: lock waits, deadlocks (lock in a consistent order), and holding locks across slow code.
Optimistic risks: wasted work and retries under high contention; you must check rowCount and handle conflict (retry or show “someone else changed this”).
Often the best answer is neither: a single conditional UPDATE or a constraint makes the race impossible.
followups: How does an HTTP ETag / If-Match relate to optimistic locking?
How do you avoid deadlocks when a transaction updates many rows?

interview.q: How would you build a reliable job queue on Postgres with many workers?
answer: Claim jobs with SELECT ... WHERE status = 'queued' ORDER BY id LIMIT n FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, so workers take different rows instead of waiting on each other.
Keep the claim transaction short: mark the job as running with a lease time, commit, then do the work outside the transaction.
A reaper returns jobs whose lease expired (crashed worker) to the queue; this makes delivery at-least-once, so handlers must be idempotent.
Index the polling query (a partial index on queued jobs) and delete or archive finished jobs to limit bloat.
Know the limits: at very high throughput, a dedicated queue is better; at moderate scale, Postgres avoids a second system and gives transactional enqueue.
followups: Why not hold the row lock for the whole job?
How do you handle a job that always fails?

one: Organising tables so each fact is stored in one place, then denormalizing deliberately where reads need it.
an: Store a customer's address once on their record, not copied onto every order, so changing it does not require hunting down 400 copies.
how: Normalized: no duplicated facts; relationships via foreign keys and joins. One-to-many (user → orders), many-to-many via a join table (students ↔ courses).
Denormalized: duplicate data on purpose for read speed (store order.total rather than summing items every time; store a comments_count).
Some duplication is correct: an order should copy the price at purchase time, because the product price will change later. That is a historical fact, not redundancy.
why: Schema mistakes are expensive to fix once data piles up. Good modeling makes most queries obvious and keeps data consistent.
trade: Every denormalized copy needs a plan for staying in sync (a transaction, a trigger, or an accepted lag).

myth.r: It is the right default. Read-heavy features often add carefully maintained denormalized fields or views.

o: Missing index
Price at purchase is historical data and should be copied onto the order item
Should use NoSQL
Isolation level
q.e: Snapshotting facts that must not change later is deliberate, correct duplication.

plain:
Normalization means storing each fact in exactly one place. A customer's address lives on the customer, not copied into every order. If it changes, you change it once.

Sometimes you copy data on purpose, either for speed or because it is history: the price on an old order must stay what the customer actually paid, even if the product price changes later.
bridge: This is the same idea as “single source of truth” in frontend state: do not store a value twice in state, derive it. Databases have the same rule, with deliberate exceptions.

walk.title: Designing orders for a shop
steps: Tables: customers, products, orders (customer_id, status, created_at), order_items (order_id, product_id, quantity).
Question: should order_items have a unit_price column, when products already has a price?
Yes. The price at purchase is a historical fact. If the product price changes tomorrow, last month's receipts must not change.
Should orders have a total column? It can be calculated from items, but the list page sums thousands of orders. Store it, and update it in the same transaction as the items.
Should orders copy the customer's email? No. That is a live fact; read it from customers.

terms: Each fact stored once, linked with IDs.
Some data copied on purpose for speed or history.
A column pointing to another table's row, checked by the DB.
A table connecting two others for many-to-many, like students ↔ courses.
insights: Normalize by default; denormalize when you can name the query it speeds up.
Every copy needs a plan for staying correct. If you cannot describe the plan, do not copy.
Snapshotting history (prices, addresses at shipping time) is not duplication. It is correctness.

prod.summary: In production, the schema is the contract that outlives every service written against it. Seniors check that each fact has one owner table, that constraints enforce the rules, that historical facts are snapshotted, and that every denormalized copy (counters, totals, cached names) has a written update path. Key choice and type sizes also matter at scale.
checklist: Each table has a primary key; IDs are bigint identity or UUIDv7, never integer for fast-growing tables.
Foreign keys exist and are indexed; ON DELETE behaviour (RESTRICT, CASCADE, SET NULL) is chosen on purpose.
Money is stored as integer minor units or numeric, never float.
Historical values (price paid, shipping address, tax rate) are copied onto the order at the time of the event.
Every denormalized field (comments_count, orders.total) is updated in the same transaction as its source, or has a documented acceptable lag and a repair job.
Soft-deleted rows do not break uniqueness: use a partial unique index WHERE deleted_at IS NULL.
Timestamps use timestamptz, not timestamp without time zone.
numbers: Postgres integer max is 2,147,483,647; a serial key on a busy events table can run out, and changing the type later rewrites the table.
bigint is 8 bytes and uuid is 16 bytes per value, in the table and in every index that contains it.
PostgreSQL 18 added a built-in uuidv7() function: time-ordered UUIDs that insert into B-tree indexes more efficiently than random UUIDv4.
failures: Inserts start failing with “integer out of range” / “nextval: reached maximum value of sequence”.
The ID column is integer and passed 2.1 billion. Migrate to bigint (new column + backfill + swap, since ALTER TYPE rewrites the table). Use bigint from day one.
Old invoices show today's product price and the accountant is upset.
Order lines join to products.price instead of storing the price paid. Add unit_price to order_items, backfill from payment records, and freeze it at checkout.
comments_count slowly drifts from the real count.
It is updated in app code outside the insert's transaction, or some paths (admin delete, cascade) skip it. Update it in the same transaction or with a trigger, and add a periodic repair query.
A user who deleted their account cannot sign up again: “duplicate key value violates unique constraint users_email_key”.
Soft delete kept the row, and the unique constraint covers deleted rows. Replace it with a partial unique index ON users (lower(email)) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL.

code.title: An order schema with deliberate snapshots and constraints
code.src:
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id           bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id  bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
  status       text   NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('pending','paid','shipped','refunded')),
  total_cents  bigint NOT NULL CHECK (total_cents >= 0),  -- denormalized, set in same tx
  ship_address jsonb  NOT NULL,                          -- snapshot at checkout
  created_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE INDEX ON orders (customer_id, created_at DESC);   -- FK index + list page

CREATE TABLE order_items (
  order_id         bigint  NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  product_id       bigint  NOT NULL REFERENCES products(id),
  quantity         integer NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0),
  unit_price_cents bigint  NOT NULL,   -- price PAID, not current price
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id)
);
CREATE INDEX ON order_items (product_id);
code.note: The composite primary key on order_items also serves as the index for lookups by order_id; product_id needs its own.

qs.s: A users table stores country_name as free text on every row. Marketing renames “Czech Republic” to “Czechia” and wants it updated everywhere. Which design would have made this a one-row change?
o: Store country as a JSON blob on each user
A countries table and a country_code foreign key on users
Index the country_name column
Store the country only in the frontend
qs.e: The country name is a fact about the country, not the user. Normalizing it into its own table means one update. An index speeds lookups but does not remove the duplication.

qs.s: A dashboard shows each project's open-task count. Counting via COUNT(*) takes 2 s for big projects. You add projects.open_tasks. Which update strategy is correct?
o: Recalculate it nightly with a cron job, and accept that it is wrong during the day
Increment/decrement it in the same transaction as task inserts and status changes, plus a periodic repair check
Update it from the frontend after each action
Cache the COUNT result in localStorage
qs.e: Changing the counter in the same transaction keeps it exactly right. A repair job catches paths someone forgot. Nightly recalculation is wrong for most of the day; frontend updates are not trusted and miss other clients.

qs.s: You need a many-to-many link between students and courses, with the enrollment date and grade. Which design is correct?
o: A course_ids integer[] array on students
A comma-separated string of course names on students
Copy the student's name into each course row
An enrollments table with student_id, course_id, enrolled_at, grade and a unique constraint on (student_id, course_id)
qs.e: Facts about the relationship (date, grade) belong to a join table. The unique constraint prevents double enrollment, and foreign keys keep both sides valid. Arrays cannot hold per-link data or enforce foreign keys.

qs.s: Read this order_items table. Which copied column is a correct, deliberate snapshot rather than harmful duplication?

code.title: order_items
code.src:
CREATE TABLE order_items (
  order_id        bigint  NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id),
  product_id      bigint  NOT NULL REFERENCES products(id),
  product_name    text    NOT NULL,  -- copied from products
  category_name   text    NOT NULL,  -- copied from categories
  supplier_email  text    NOT NULL,  -- copied from suppliers
  unit_price_paid bigint  NOT NULL,  -- copied from products.price
  quantity        integer NOT NULL
);

o: supplier_email, so emails are faster to send
category_name, so reports can group by category without a join
All of them, because orders are historical

unit_price_paid: the price at purchase is a fact about the order that must not change; the others are live facts that should be read from their own tables (product name is a judgment call for invoices)
qs.e: Ask “should this value change on old orders when the source changes?”. The price paid: never. A supplier's email: you want the current one. Category name: reports usually want today's category. Copying “everything because orders are historical” creates many fields with no update plan. Invoices sometimes snapshot the product name too, on purpose.

qs.s: Comments can belong to a post, a photo or a video. This design is used. What problem will appear in production?

code.title: comments

o: It cannot store more than three types

commentable_id cannot have a foreign key, so deleting a post leaves orphan comments and typos in the type are accepted; use one nullable FK column per parent with a CHECK that exactly one is set, or one comment table per parent
Queries by type are impossible
bigint is too small for IDs from three tables
qs.e: A foreign key points to one table, so a “polymorphic” column cannot be checked by the database. Separate columns (post_id, photo_id, video_id) with CHECK (num_nonnulls(post_id, photo_id, video_id) = 1) keep real FKs and cascades. Queries by type work fine, so that is not the issue.

qs.s: A team stores product attributes in an entity-attribute-value table: product_attrs(product_id, attr_name, attr_value text). Search “red shoes, size 42, under 2 kg” is slow and type bugs appear (“42” vs 42). What is the usual better design in Postgres?
o: Real columns for attributes every product has, and a jsonb column with a GIN index for category-specific ones
Add an index on attr_value
Move to a graph database
Store all attributes in one comma-separated text column
qs.e: EAV needs one self-join per condition, has no types and no constraints. Common attributes become typed columns with CHECK constraints; truly variable ones go into JSONB, which supports containment queries (@>) with one index. An index on attr_value still leaves the self-joins and type problems.

qs.s: A table will hold 1 billion rows. The primary key appears in the table and in 3 other indexes on it. Roughly how much extra storage does uuid (16 bytes) cost compared with bigint (8 bytes) for the key values alone?
o: About 8 GB
About 16 GB
About 32 GB
About 64 GB
qs.e: 8 extra bytes × 1,000,000,000 rows × 4 places (table + 3 indexes) = 32 GB, before alignment padding and before foreign key columns in other tables that also store it. That is not a reason to ban UUIDs, but it is a real cost to weigh against their benefits (IDs generated anywhere, not guessable).

interview.q: Design the core schema for an online shop's orders. What do you normalize and what do you copy?
answer: Tables: customers, products, orders, order_items, payments; foreign keys indexed, bigint identity or UUIDv7 keys.
Normalize live facts: customer email, product description, category; they are read via joins.
Snapshot historical facts on the order: unit price paid, tax rate, currency, shipping address at checkout.
Denormalize for speed only with an update plan: orders.total_cents written in the same transaction as the items, with a CHECK and a repair query.
Money as integer minor units or numeric; status as a CHECK or enum; timestamps as timestamptz.
Constraints carry the rules (quantity > 0, one row per order+product, NOT NULL), not only app code.
followups: How would you handle refunds of part of an order?
How would multi-currency change this design?

interview.q: When do you denormalize, and how do you keep the copy correct?
answer: When a specific, measured query is too slow or too frequent with joins or aggregates (counters, totals, list pages).
Name the owner of the truth; the copy is derived from it.
Update paths in order of strength: same transaction, a trigger, an outbox/CDC consumer with accepted lag.
Add a repair job that recomputes and compares, plus a metric for drift.
Consider alternatives first: a better index, a materialized view refreshed on a schedule, or a cache.
followups: Trigger vs app code for keeping a counter: which and why?
How would a hot counter row affect concurrency?

interview.q: UUID or bigint for primary keys? Defend your choice.
answer: bigint identity: 8 bytes, sequential (good index locality), simple; but IDs are guessable and need the database to generate them.
UUIDv4: generated anywhere, not guessable, safe to merge across systems; but 16 bytes and random inserts hurt B-tree cache locality at scale.
UUIDv7: time-ordered, so it keeps insert locality while still generated anywhere; built-in uuidv7() in Postgres 18. It reveals creation time.
Never use integer (4 bytes) for tables that grow fast; changing the type later rewrites the table.
A common pattern: bigint internal key plus a separate public random ID for URLs.
followups: Why does insert order matter for a B-tree?
Is exposing sequential IDs in URLs a security bug?
