one: Versioned scripts that evolve the database schema step by step, run the same way in every environment.
an: Git commits for your database structure.
how: Each migration is a file (0042_add_phone_to_users.sql) applied in order; the DB records which ones ran. Tools: Prisma Migrate, Flyway, Alembic, Rails, Knex, Drizzle.
Zero-downtime changes use expand → migrate → contract: add the new column (nullable), deploy code writing both, backfill old rows in batches, switch reads, then drop the old column in a later deploy.

Some operations rewrite or lock big tables: adding a column with a volatile default like clock_timestamp() (any version; a constant default is instant since Postgres 11), creating an index without CONCURRENTLY, changing a column type, or adding NOT NULL directly (a full scan while holding an exclusive lock).
why: During a rolling deploy, old and new code run at the same time against one schema. Migrations must be compatible with both versions.
trade: "Down" migrations are rarely trustworthy once data has changed. Plan to roll forward instead, and take backups before risky changes.

myth.m: Renaming a column is a one-line migration.
myth.r: The old code still running during the deploy reads the old name and crashes. It is a multi-step change.

q.s: You add CREATE INDEX on a 200M-row orders table during business hours and checkout freezes. What should you have used in Postgres?
o: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY
A bigger server
A NoSQL DB
A transaction
q.e: A plain CREATE INDEX blocks writes to the table until it finishes. CONCURRENTLY builds it without blocking writes (slower, cannot run inside a transaction).

more: Lock levels per ALTER TABLE operation
lock_timeout and statement_timeout as safety rails during migrations
Backfilling in batches without long transactions
Adding NOT NULL safely (CHECK NOT VALID → VALIDATE)
Migration ordering across code deploys
lab: Using your ORM's migration tool, rename a column with expand/migrate/contract across three migrations and two app versions.
Create an index with and without CONCURRENTLY on a large table while another session inserts in a loop. Compare.
Set SET lock_timeout = '2s' before a migration and simulate a blocking long transaction to see it fail fast instead of freezing the app.

plain:
Your database structure changes as the app grows: new tables, new columns, new indexes. A migration is a small script for one such change, saved in your repo and run in the same order everywhere (your laptop, staging, production).

The tricky part is production: changes must not lock big tables for minutes, and they must work while old and new app versions run at the same time during a deploy.
bridge: Migrations are git commits for your database schema. prisma migrate dev or drizzle-kit generate creates them; your deploy runs them.

walk.title: Making a column required without downtime
steps: Goal: every user must have a phone. Today the column does not exist.
Migration 1: add phone as nullable. Fast and safe. Deploy app code that writes phone for new users.
Backfill: a script fills phone for old users in batches of 1,000, so no long locks.
Migration 2: add CHECK (phone IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID (instant), then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT, which scans the table without blocking writes. Then SET NOT NULL sees the valid check and skips its own scan.

If you had added phone NOT NULL in one step, it would fail (existing rows have no value) or force a default you do not want, and a direct SET NOT NULL on a big table blocks all reads and writes while it scans.

terms: A versioned script that changes the database structure.
Filling a new column for existing rows.
The DB blocking other work on a table while it changes.
Add new structure, move to it, then remove the old.
insights: During a deploy, old and new code run at the same time. Every migration must work with both.
Creating an index on a big Postgres table needs CONCURRENTLY, or writes stop until it finishes.
Plan to fix forward. “Down” migrations rarely undo data changes correctly.

prod.summary: In production, a migration is a deploy step that can take the whole app down: one ALTER TABLE waiting for a lock queues every query behind it. Seniors read every migration for lock level and duration, set lock_timeout, split risky changes into expand/contract steps, and make sure each step works with both the old and the new app version running at the same time.
checklist: Every migration sets SET lock_timeout = '5s' (or similar) and is retried, so it fails fast instead of queueing all traffic behind it.
Indexes on existing tables use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, outside a transaction block (many tools need a “no transaction” flag for this file).
New constraints on big tables are added NOT VALID and validated in a separate step.
No rename or drop of a column that the currently deployed code still reads; renames are add + backfill + switch + drop.
Backfills run in batches (by primary key range) outside the migration, with a pause between batches to limit replica lag.
Migrations run once per deploy (a single job or init step), not in every app replica at startup.
The migration was tested on a copy of production-size data, and its run time is known.
numbers: Since Postgres 11, ADD COLUMN ... DEFAULT with a constant is metadata-only and instant; a volatile default such as clock_timestamp() still rewrites the table.
Postgres lock_timeout and statement_timeout default to 0 (wait forever).
VALIDATE CONSTRAINT takes only a SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE lock, so normal reads and writes continue during the scan.
failures: A deploy runs ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN ... and the whole API times out for 3 minutes, although the ALTER itself is instant.

The ALTER waited for an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock behind a long-running query, and every new query queued behind the ALTER. Set lock_timeout (a few seconds) and retry; find and kill the long transaction first.
After deploy, the old pods log “column users.name does not exist” for 2 minutes.
The migration renamed or dropped a column while old code was still running in a rolling deploy. Use expand/contract: add the new column, write both, switch reads, drop in a later release.
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction block in CI.
The migration tool wraps each file in a transaction. Put the concurrent index in its own migration with the tool's no-transaction option.
A backfill UPDATE users SET phone_e164 = ... on 40M rows causes replica lag of 15 minutes and stale reads.
One huge update generates a big burst of WAL. Backfill in batches of a few thousand rows, commit each, and pause when replica lag exceeds a threshold.

code.title: Adding NOT NULL to a big table safely
code.note: If any step hits lock_timeout, it fails cleanly and you retry later, instead of freezing traffic behind a queued lock.

qs.s: You want to rename users.fullname to users.display_name in a Kubernetes app with rolling deploys. Which sequence is safe?
o: One migration: ALTER TABLE RENAME COLUMN, deployed with the new code
Rename the column first, deploy code a day later
Add display_name; deploy code that writes both and reads the old one; backfill; deploy code that reads display_name; later drop fullname
Create a new users table and switch over in one deploy
qs.e: During a rolling deploy, old and new pods run together. Expand/contract keeps every intermediate state valid for both versions. A one-step rename breaks whichever version expects the other name.

qs.s: A migration ALTER TABLE payments ADD COLUMN note text is normally instant, but in production it hangs and the checkout API stops responding. pg_stat_activity shows an analytics query running for 20 minutes on payments. What happened?
o: Adding a text column rewrites the table
The ALTER is waiting for an exclusive lock behind the analytics query, and all new queries are queued behind the ALTER
The column name is reserved
The connection pool is too small
qs.e: ALTER TABLE needs an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock even for instant changes. Lock requests queue in order, so everything after the ALTER waits too. lock_timeout makes it give up and retry instead of blocking checkout.

qs.s: Which of these Postgres 17 changes on a 300M-row table is safe to run directly during business hours?
o: ALTER TABLE t ADD COLUMN flag boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false
ALTER TABLE t ALTER COLUMN id TYPE bigint
CREATE INDEX t_x_idx ON t (x)
ALTER TABLE t ADD COLUMN created_at timestamptz DEFAULT clock_timestamp()
qs.e: A constant default is stored in metadata since Postgres 11, so this is instant (still set lock_timeout). Changing the type rewrites the table, a plain CREATE INDEX blocks writes, and a volatile default like clock_timestamp() forces a full rewrite.

qs.s: This migration adds a column and fills it in one file. On a 50M-row table, the API is down for 20 minutes. Why?

code.title: 0042_add_region.sql

o: Adding a nullable text column rewrites the whole table
The ALTER takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, which is held until COMMIT, so every read and write on users waits for both full-table UPDATEs
The UPDATEs need an index on country
The migration should use Serializable
qs.e: Locks are held until the end of the transaction. The ALTER itself is instant, but its exclusive lock now covers the slow backfill too. Put the ALTER in its own migration with a lock_timeout, and run the backfill separately in small batches. Adding a nullable column without a default is metadata-only.

qs.s: Every pod runs migrations at startup. What is the main problem with this setup?

code.title: deployment.yaml (excerpt)
code.src:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  replicas: 6
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: api
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: registry.example.com/api:1.42.0
          command: ["sh", "-c", "npm run migrate && node dist/server.js"]

o: Kubernetes does not allow shell commands in containers
Migrations will run in the wrong order
Nothing; migration tools take a lock, so this is the recommended pattern

Six pods race to migrate (and every restart or scale-up runs it again); a slow migration delays readiness and a failing one crash-loops every pod. Run migrations once per release as a separate Job/pipeline step before the rollout
qs.e: Many tools do take an advisory lock, so the race may not corrupt anything; that is why the “recommended” option is tempting. But the coupling stays: autoscaling events and restarts start migrations, pods block on each other, and one bad migration takes down all replicas instead of failing one deploy step.

qs.s: You want to drop users.legacy_score. No code reads it any more, but the ORM loads all columns it knows from a schema cached at startup. Rolling deploy. Safe order?
o: Deploy code that tells the ORM to ignore the column; after all old pods are gone, drop the column in a later migration
Drop the column and deploy the new code in the same release
Drop the column first, then deploy code
Rename it to _legacy_score and drop it a week later in the same deploy as the code
qs.e: Old pods still running during the rollout would select or insert the column and fail with “column does not exist”. Contract steps go in the order: stop using it everywhere (including ORM metadata), make sure no old version runs, then drop. Renaming first breaks old code exactly like dropping.

qs.s: You need a foreign key from orders.customer_id (400M rows) to customers.id. Which sequence avoids a long blocking scan?
o: ALTER TABLE orders ADD FOREIGN KEY ... in one statement during low traffic
Create a trigger that checks each new row instead
ADD CONSTRAINT ... FOREIGN KEY ... NOT VALID (checks only new rows, quick), then later VALIDATE CONSTRAINT, which scans with a weaker lock
Drop the index on customer_id first to make validation faster
qs.e: Adding a foreign key normally scans all existing rows while holding a lock that blocks writes on orders. NOT VALID skips that scan, and VALIDATE takes only SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE on the table it checks, so writes continue. Doing it “during low traffic” still blocks writes for the whole scan.

interview.q: How do you rename a column with zero downtime?
answer: Never in one step: during a rolling deploy, old and new code run together against one schema.
Expand: add the new column (nullable). Deploy code that writes both columns and still reads the old one.
Migrate: backfill old rows in batches by primary key range, with pauses to limit lock time and replica lag.
Switch: deploy code that reads the new column (still writing both, so a rollback works).
Contract: stop writing the old column, wait until no old version runs, then drop it in a later release.
Cost: 3–4 deploys; for low-traffic internal tables a short maintenance window can be a fair trade-off.
followups: How would you keep the two columns in sync for writes you do not control, like other services?
How do you verify the backfill is complete?

interview.q: How do you make sure a migration does not take production down?
answer: Review each statement for its lock level and whether it rewrites or scans the table (type change, volatile default, plain CREATE INDEX, SET NOT NULL, new FK).
Set lock_timeout (seconds) so a lock wait fails fast instead of queueing all traffic, and retry.
Use the safe forms: CONCURRENTLY indexes, NOT VALID + VALIDATE constraints, batched backfills outside the migration.
Test on a production-size copy and know the runtime; check for long-running transactions before starting.
Run migrations once as a deploy step, with monitoring of lock waits and replica lag while it runs.
followups: Why can an “instant” ALTER still cause an outage?
Would you run migrations before or after deploying the new code?

interview.q: A migration failed halfway in production. What do you do?
answer: First, find out the current state: which statements ran, whether the tool marked the migration as applied, and whether the app is healthy.

On Postgres most DDL is transactional, so a migration in one transaction is fully rolled back; non-transactional steps (CONCURRENTLY, some tools' multi-file runs) can leave partial state such as an INVALID index.
Prefer rolling forward: write a new migration that brings the schema to a known good state, instead of hand-editing or trusting a down script.
Make migrations idempotent where possible (IF NOT EXISTS) so a rerun is safe.
Afterwards: add the missing guard (lock_timeout, test on prod-size data, split the step).
followups: Why are down migrations rarely trusted?
How would you handle a failed data backfill?

diagrams.title: Why an “instant” ALTER can freeze the API
diagrams.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant R as Report query
  participant M as Migration
  participant API as API queries

  M->>PG: ALTER TABLE orders (needs ACCESS EXCLUSIVE)
  Note over M,PG: ALTER waits behind the report

one: Keeping copies of the database on other machines, for failover and to spread read load.
an: A head chef (primary) who writes the recipes, and assistants (replicas) who copy each change into their own books and answer questions from them.
how: Writes go to the primary. It streams its change log to replicas, which apply it. Reads can go to replicas.
Asynchronous replication (common) means replicas lag by milliseconds to seconds. Synchronous waits for a replica to confirm, so it is safer and slower.

If the primary dies, a replica is promoted (failover). Some managed options automate this, for example Amazon RDS Multi-AZ and Cloud SQL high availability; on others (and with self-hosted Postgres plus a tool like Patroni) you must check what is automatic and how long it takes.
why: Read-heavy apps scale reads cheaply, and you survive a machine failure without losing the service.
trade: Replication lag causes "I saved it but it is not there" bugs. Fix with read-your-own-writes: route a user's reads to the primary for a few seconds after they write, or for that specific screen.

myth.r: A replica faithfully copies your mistakes. DROP TABLE replicates in milliseconds. You still need point-in-time backups.

q.s: After editing their profile, users sometimes see the old version on the next page. Reads go to replicas. Fix?
o: Disable caching
Read from the primary for that user shortly after they write (read-your-writes)
Add another replica
Shard
q.e: The replica has not caught up yet. Routing that user's next reads to the primary hides the lag where it matters.

plain:
Replication keeps copies of your database on other machines. One machine (the primary) takes all the writes and sends every change to the copies (replicas).

Replicas give you two things: a backup machine ready to take over if the primary dies, and extra machines to answer read queries. The catch: replicas are usually a little behind.
bridge: You may have seen “I saved my profile, refreshed, and it showed the old value for a second.” That is often replication lag: the save went to the primary, the refresh read from a replica that had not caught up yet.

walk.title: Read-your-own-writes in practice
steps: Writes go to the primary; reads go to two replicas to spread load.
A user changes their display name. The write hits the primary at 12:00:00.000.
The page reloads at 12:00:00.050 and reads from a replica that is 200ms behind. It shows the old name.
Fix: after a user writes, send that user's reads to the primary for the next few seconds (store a timestamp in their session).
Other users reading from replicas may see the new name 200ms later, which nobody notices.

terms: A copy that receives changes from the primary; usually read-only.
How far behind a replica is.
Promoting a replica to be the new primary when the old one fails.
insights: Decide per screen whether stale data is acceptable. “Balance after a transfer” must read the primary; “list of venues” can read a replica.
Failover is only as fast as your app's reconnect. Test it, including DNS caching and dead pooled connections.
A replication slot that nobody reads keeps WAL forever and can fill the primary's disk.

prod.summary: In production, replicas serve two different goals that need different setups: high availability (a standby ready to take over) and read scaling (replicas that answer queries). Seniors decide which reads may be stale, measure lag in seconds and bytes, watch replication slots that can fill the primary's disk, and rehearse failover, because apps that cache DNS or hold old connections often fail long after the database recovered.
checklist: Each read path is labelled: may be stale (lists, search, reports) or must be fresh (after-write views, balances, auth checks); only the first kind goes to replicas.
Alert on replica lag (pg_stat_replication.replay_lag on the primary, or now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() on the replica) above a few seconds.
Alert on retained WAL for replication slots; set max_slot_wal_keep_size so an abandoned slot cannot fill the disk.
Point-in-time backups exist and are restore-tested separately from replicas.
Failover was tested in staging: the app reconnects, the pool drops dead connections, and DNS TTL is short (AWS recommends at most 60s for JVM DNS caching).
Long analytics queries on a replica are either moved to a dedicated replica or the conflict settings (max_standby_streaming_delay, hot_standby_feedback) are tuned on purpose.
Writes accidentally sent to a replica fail loudly (they do: “cannot execute INSERT in a read-only transaction”), and the router is tested.
numbers: Amazon RDS Multi-AZ (single standby) failover typically takes 60–120 seconds, and the standby cannot serve reads.
Postgres max_standby_streaming_delay defaults to 30s: after that, replica queries that conflict with replay are cancelled. hot_standby_feedback defaults to off.
Postgres max_slot_wal_keep_size defaults to -1 (unlimited), so an inactive replication slot can keep WAL until the primary's disk is full.
failures: Reports on the replica fail with “canceling statement due to conflict with recovery”.

Vacuum on the primary removed rows the long query still needs, and the replica cancelled the query after max_standby_streaming_delay (30s). Use a separate reporting replica with a larger delay, or enable hot_standby_feedback (at the cost of bloat on the primary).
The primary's disk fills up overnight; pg_wal is hundreds of GB.
A replication slot for a dead replica or a stopped CDC consumer keeps all WAL. Drop the slot (pg_drop_replication_slot), and set max_slot_wal_keep_size plus an alert on slot lag.
Users save a form, get redirected, and see the old data about 1 time in 20.
Reads go to an async replica that lags 100–500 ms. Route reads to the primary for that user for a few seconds after a write, or for the after-write page.
Database failover finished in 90 seconds, but the API returned errors for 15 minutes.
App instances kept dead pooled connections or cached the old IP from DNS. Set pool connection validation/short idle timeouts, a short DNS TTL, and retry on connection errors; rehearse failover.

code.title: Measuring replication lag and slot risk
code.src:
-- On the PRIMARY: one row per connected replica
SELECT application_name, state,
       write_lag, flush_lag, replay_lag,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), replay_lsn)) AS behind
FROM pg_stat_replication;

-- On the PRIMARY: WAL kept back by each replication slot
SELECT slot_name, active,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn)) AS retained
FROM pg_replication_slots;

-- On a REPLICA: time since the last replayed transaction
-- (grows on an idle primary too, so compare with write traffic)
SELECT now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() AS replay_delay;
code.note: An inactive slot with growing retained is the classic “disk full on the primary” incident in progress.

qs.s: A product wants “never lose a committed payment, even if the primary's disk dies”. Replication is asynchronous with a 50 ms average lag. What does that mean for the requirement?
o: It is met; 50 ms is tiny
It is only a problem with logical replication
It is met because WAL is fsynced on the primary

It is not met: transactions committed in the last moments before the crash may not have reached the replica; use synchronous replication (or a managed option with synchronous standby) for that guarantee
qs.e: Async replication confirms the commit before the replica has the data. If the primary's storage is lost, the newest commits are gone. Synchronous commit to a standby closes that gap at the cost of write latency.

qs.s: You move all GET endpoints to read replicas. A user changes their password and is immediately asked to log in again, and the login fails with “wrong password” about 5% of the time. What is the right fix?
o: Send auth and after-write reads to the primary; keep staleness-tolerant reads on replicas
Add more replicas
Increase the session cookie lifetime
Switch to logical replication
qs.e: Authentication must read fresh data. Classify reads: auth, balances and after-write pages go to the primary. More replicas do not reduce lag.

qs.s: Logical replication to an analytics system was paused for a weekend. On Monday the primary is at 97% disk. What is the most likely cause?
o: Analytics queries are running on the primary
Autovacuum is disabled
The logical replication slot kept all WAL since Friday because the consumer stopped reading
Indexes on the primary grew
qs.e: A slot guarantees WAL is kept until its consumer confirms it. A paused consumer means WAL grows without limit (default max_slot_wal_keep_size = -1). Alert on slot retention and set a limit.

qs.s: Read the output from the primary. What does it tell you about replica-2?
o: The network between the primary and replica-2 is slow
replica-2 has lost its connection and must be rebuilt

replica-2 receives and saves WAL quickly but is 42 s behind in applying it, typically because replay is paused by a conflicting long query (up to max_standby_streaming_delay) or the replica's disk/CPU is overloaded
replica-2 is a synchronous standby
qs.e: write_lag and flush_lag are about 2 ms, so the network and the replica's WAL writes are fine. Only replay_lag is large, so the delay is in applying changes. A long report on that replica is the most common cause. Stale reads from replica-2 are 42 seconds old right now.

qs.s: This code implements read-your-own-writes. The API runs 8 instances behind a load balancer without sticky sessions. Users still see stale data after saving. Why?

code.title: db-router.ts

o: 5 seconds is too short

The write timestamp lives in one instance's memory; the user's next request usually hits another instance, which routes to the replica. Store it where every instance sees it (a cookie or session), or compare the replica's replay position
Map is not thread-safe in Node.js
The primary is too slow
qs.e: With 8 instances the follow-up read lands on the same one only about 1 time in 8. Put the “last write” marker in the user's cookie/session, or store the commit LSN and only read from a replica that has replayed past it. Node runs JS on one thread, so the Map is not the issue.

qs.s: The primary has synchronous_standby_names = 'FIRST 1 (replica1)' and synchronous_commit = on. replica1's host dies. What do users see?
o: Every write transaction hangs at COMMIT, waiting for a standby that is gone, until the setting is changed or replica1 returns
Nothing; Postgres automatically falls back to async
The primary promotes another replica
Reads fail but writes continue
qs.e: Postgres does not fall back to async on its own. The commit is written locally but the client waits for the standby's confirmation. With two or more candidates, ANY 1 (replica1, replica2) survives one failure. Managed services handle this for you; self-hosted setups must plan it.

qs.s: You must upgrade a 3 TB Postgres 14 database to 17 with only a few minutes of downtime. Which replication approach fits?
o: Streaming (physical) replication to a 17 replica, then promote it
Take a pg_dump and restore it during the maintenance window
Synchronous replication
Logical replication from 14 to a new 17 server, let it catch up, then switch the app over
qs.e: Physical replication copies the on-disk format and works only between the same major version. Logical replication sends row changes, so it works across versions. Watch its limits: sequences and DDL are not replicated, and tables need a primary key or replica identity for updates and deletes. A dump of 3 TB takes hours.

interview.q: You are adding read replicas to an existing app. What changes in the code and in operations?
answer: Classify reads: stale-OK (lists, search, reports) go to replicas; must-be-fresh (after-write pages, auth, balances, anything that decides a write) go to the primary.
Implement read-your-own-writes with a marker shared by all instances (session/cookie or LSN), not instance memory.
Two pools (primary and replica); writes on a replica fail with a read-only error, so routing bugs show up fast in tests.
Monitor replay lag and alert; consider taking a lagging replica out of the read pool automatically.
Long analytics on replicas can be cancelled by replay conflicts; give them their own replica.
followups: How would you route reads inside an ORM?
What happens to the replica pool during failover?

interview.q: Compare synchronous and asynchronous replication. How do RPO and RTO fit in?
answer: RPO (recovery point objective): how much recent data you may lose. RTO (recovery time objective): how long recovery may take.
Async: commits return before replicas have the data; low write latency; if the primary's storage is lost, the last moments of commits can be lost (RPO > 0).
Sync: commit waits for a standby's confirmation; RPO about 0 for that standby; each commit pays a network round trip, and a dead standby can block writes unless you have quorum (ANY 1 (a, b)).
RTO depends on failover detection and promotion plus app reconnection, often a minute or more on managed services.
Replicas never replace backups: point-in-time recovery covers mistakes like a bad DELETE.
followups: Would you put a synchronous standby in another region?
What is split-brain and how is it prevented?

interview.q: Walk me through what happens during a database failover and how the application should behave.
answer: The primary fails; the orchestrator (managed service, Patroni) detects it after health-check timeouts, fences the old primary and promotes a standby.
The endpoint moves (DNS change or virtual IP); clients holding old connections get errors.
App: drop broken pooled connections, reconnect with backoff, respect a short DNS TTL, and retry idempotent operations.
Writes in flight may fail; with async replication some recently committed ones may be lost.
Rehearse it: many outages last longer in the app (cached IPs, stuck pools) than in the database.
followups: How do you make retries after failover safe for payments?
How long does failover take on your current platform, and how did you measure it?

one: Splitting one big dataset into pieces. Partitioning splits a table within one database; sharding spreads data across several database servers.
an: One library becomes several branches, each holding authors A–F, G–M, and so on. Each branch is smaller and faster, but a query across all authors now visits every branch.
how: Partitioning (one server): e.g. Postgres splits events by month. Old months can be dropped instantly; queries on recent data touch less.

Sharding (many servers): pick a shard key (tenant_id, user_id). A router sends each query to the right shard. Hash-based keys spread evenly; range-based keys keep neighbours together but can create hot spots.
Cross-shard joins and transactions become hard or impossible.
why: When one machine cannot hold the data or absorb the writes, there is no other way. It is a common system-design interview topic.
trade: It is the last resort: indexes, caching, read replicas, bigger machines and archiving come first. A bad shard key (celebrity user, one giant tenant) creates a hot shard, and resharding later is painful.

myth.m: We should shard early to be ready for scale.
myth.r: Sharding adds permanent complexity. A single modern Postgres box handles terabytes and thousands of writes per second.

q.s: A multi-tenant SaaS shards by tenant_id. One enterprise tenant is 40% of all traffic. What problem is this?
o: Replication lag
A hot shard: the key does not spread load evenly
CORS
q.e: Shard keys must spread load. Large tenants may need a dedicated shard or a finer key.

Partition pruning in query plans
Citus and Vitess as sharding layers
Global unique IDs across shards (Snowflake IDs, UUIDv7)
Resharding strategies
lab: Create an events table partitioned by month in Postgres. Insert a year of data.
Run EXPLAIN on a query for one month and confirm only one partition is scanned.
Drop the oldest partition and note how instant it is compared to DELETE.

plain:
When one table gets huge, you can split it. Partitioning splits it into pieces inside the same database (for example, one piece per month). Sharding spreads the data across several database servers (for example, users A–M on server 1, N–Z on server 2).

Sharding lets you grow almost without limit, but queries across shards and transactions across shards become very hard.
bridge: It is like splitting one giant JSON file into one file per user: each file is small and fast, but answering “how many users bought X?” now means opening every file.

walk.title: Partitioning event logs by month
steps: An events table grows by 50 million rows a month. Queries for “last 7 days” get slower every week.
You partition it by month: events_2026_09, events_2026_10, and so on, under one parent table.
A query for the last 7 days now only reads the current month's partition (partition pruning).
Deleting data older than a year becomes DROP TABLE events_2025_09: instant, instead of a huge slow DELETE.
No application code changed, and you are still on one database server. Sharding would only come much later, if ever.

terms: A piece of a table, stored separately but queried as one.
A piece of the data living on its own database server.
The field deciding which shard a row goes to (e.g. tenant_id).
A shard receiving far more traffic than the others.
insights: Partition big time-based tables early; it is cheap. Shard across servers late; it is expensive and permanent.
Pick the shard key from your main queries: if almost every query filters by tenant_id, that is your key.
Plan how to move one tenant that outgrows its shard before it happens.

prod.summary: In production, partitioning is a routine tool for big time-based tables (logs, events, metrics), while sharding across servers is a major architecture decision you live with for years. Seniors exhaust the cheaper options first, and when they shard, they choose a key that matches the main queries, keeps related data on one shard (usually tenant_id), and plan for one tenant outgrowing a shard.
checklist: Before sharding: query tuning, indexes, read replicas, caching, archiving cold data and a bigger instance were tried and measured.
Partitioned tables: every hot query filters on the partition key so the plan shows partition pruning.
Future partitions are created ahead of time (a scheduled job or pg_partman), with an alert if fewer than N future partitions exist.

A DEFAULT partition is a deliberate choice: it catches stray rows, but it blocks DETACH PARTITION ... CONCURRENTLY, and creating a new partition must scan it and fails if it holds rows for that range.
Old data is removed by detaching and dropping partitions, not with huge DELETEs.
The shard key appears in almost every query; queries without it are listed and either avoided or sent to a separate analytics store.
IDs are globally unique across shards (UUIDv7, Snowflake-style IDs), not per-shard sequences.
There is a plan to move one large tenant to its own shard without downtime.
numbers: Postgres declarative partitioning supports range, list and hash partitioning (hash since Postgres 11).
ALTER TABLE ... DETACH PARTITION ... CONCURRENTLY has been available since Postgres 14; it cannot run in a transaction block or when a default partition exists.
Elasticsearch index.number_of_shards defaults to 1 and cannot be changed after the index is created (you reindex or use split/shrink).
A DynamoDB partition serves up to 3,000 read units and 1,000 write units per second, so one hot key is capped regardless of table capacity.
failures: A query on a partitioned events table is slower than before partitioning; the plan scans all 36 partitions.

The query does not filter on the partition key (e.g. it filters by user_id only, partitioned by created_at). Add a time range to the query, or rethink the key; pruning only happens on the partition key.
At midnight on the 1st of the month, inserts fail with “no partition of relation "events" found for row”.

The next month's partition was not created. Create partitions several periods ahead with a scheduled job or pg_partman, and alert when the number of future partitions drops. A DEFAULT partition prevents the error, but see its costs above.
The nightly job fails with “cannot detach partitions concurrently when a default partition exists”.

Someone added a DEFAULT partition as a safety net. Either remove it (move its rows into proper partitions first) or use a plain DETACH PARTITION, which takes a stronger lock on the parent, with a short lock_timeout and retries.
One shard is at 90% CPU while the others sit at 20%.
A hot shard: one large tenant or a range key concentrating new writes. Move that tenant to a dedicated shard, or use a hash of a finer key; check traffic share per key before choosing it.
A “top products across all customers” report takes minutes after sharding by tenant.
It is a scatter-gather query across every shard. Serve cross-tenant analytics from a warehouse fed by CDC, not from the sharded OLTP cluster.

code.title: Monthly range partitioning in Postgres
code.note: Primary keys and unique constraints on a partitioned table must include the partition key, which is why created_at is in the PK. DETACH ... CONCURRENTLY is not allowed when the table has a default partition, so this design relies on creating partitions ahead and alerting if that job fails.

qs.s: A B2B SaaS shards by tenant_id hash. Almost every query is “within one tenant”. A new feature needs “search users across all tenants by email” for the login page. Best approach?
o: Query every shard on each login
Reshard by email
Keep a small global lookup table (email → tenant_id, shard) outside the shards, then query one shard
Disable sharding for the users table only by copying it to every shard
qs.e: A global directory is the standard answer for the few queries that do not carry the shard key. Fan-out on every login gets slower as shards grow, and resharding by email would break every tenant-scoped query.

qs.s: A Postgres metrics table gets 30M rows/day; queries are always for the last 24 hours; data older than 90 days is deleted nightly with DELETE and the table is bloated. Best change?
o: Shard across 4 servers
Partition by day (range on created_at) and drop old partitions instead of DELETE
Add more indexes
Partition by hash of metric_id
qs.e: Time-range queries and time-based retention match range partitioning: queries prune to 1–2 partitions, and dropping a partition is instant with no bloat. Hash partitioning would spread one day across all partitions and gives no cheap retention.

qs.s: You choose created_at month as the shard key for an orders system across 4 servers. What problem appears first?
o: All new writes go to the one shard holding the current month, so it is a write hot spot while the others are idle
Joins between orders and order_items break
IDs collide
Reads become strongly consistent
qs.e: A monotonically increasing range key sends all current traffic to one shard. Range keys suit partitioning for retention on one server, but for spreading load across servers you want a hash or tenant-based key.

qs.s: You partition users by hash of id and run this. What happens?

code.title: users.sql

o: It works; each partition enforces email uniqueness globally
It fails: a unique constraint on a partitioned table must include all partition key columns, and UNIQUE (email) does not include id
It works, but uniqueness is only checked within each partition
It fails because hash partitioning does not support primary keys
qs.e: Postgres enforces uniqueness per partition, so it can only guarantee global uniqueness when the constraint includes the partition key. Postgres rejects the table instead of silently checking per partition. For a global unique email, keep a separate non-partitioned lookup table, or partition by a key the constraint includes.

qs.s: Read the router. The team adds a 5th shard to the existing 4. What happens to existing data?

code.title: shard-router.ts

o: Only new tenants go to shard 5; existing ones stay where they are
About 20% of tenants move to the new shard
Nothing moves because SHA-1 is stable
Changing % 4 to % 5 changes the shard for about 80% of tenants, so most reads go to a shard without their data until everything is migrated; use a directory table or consistent hashing
qs.e: With modulo, a key stays on the same shard only if h % 4 == h % 5, which is true for about 1 in 5 keys. A directory (tenant → shard table) lets you move tenants one at a time. Consistent hashing moves only about 1/5 of keys when adding the fifth node. “About 20% move” is what people expect, but that is the consistent-hashing result.

qs.s: A dashboard query fans out to 16 shards and waits for all of them. Each shard answers within 50 ms in 99% of requests. Roughly what share of dashboard requests take longer than 50 ms?
o: About 1%
About 15%
About 50%
About 99%
qs.e: The request is fast only if all 16 shards are fast: 0.99<sup>16</sup> ≈ 0.85, so about 15% are slower than 50 ms. Fan-out turns each shard's rare slow response into a common one for the whole request (tail latency). This is a strong reason to keep hot queries on one shard.

qs.s: Users are sharded by user_id. A transfer moves money from a user on shard 1 to a user on shard 3. How should it be built?
o: One BEGIN ... COMMIT that spans both shards' connections
Debit on shard 1, credit on shard 3, and hope neither fails

As a saga: record the transfer and debit on shard 1 with an outbox event in one local transaction, then credit on shard 3 idempotently (keyed by transfer ID), with a compensating step if the credit is rejected
Move both users to the same shard before every transfer
qs.e: A transaction belongs to one connection on one server, so two separate COMMITs are not atomic together; a crash between them loses money. Two-phase commit exists (PREPARE TRANSACTION) but is rarely used in apps because of blocking and operations. A saga with an outbox and idempotent steps gives eventual consistency you can reason about.

interview.q: Our Postgres primary is at 85% CPU and growing 10% a month. Should we shard? Walk me through your thinking.
answer: First find where the CPU goes: pg_stat_statements by total time; often a few queries dominate and need indexes or rewrites.
Remove load that does not need the primary: reads that tolerate lag to replicas, reports to a warehouse, hot reads to a cache.
Reduce data: partition and drop old data, archive cold rows.
Scale up: a bigger instance buys time cheaply; check headroom for another 12–24 months.
Shard only if writes or data size will still exceed one machine; choose the key from the main access pattern, and consider Citus or a managed distributed Postgres before building a router.
Present it as a cost: cross-shard queries, transactions, resharding and operations are permanent.
followups: What metrics would convince you sharding is necessary?
How would you split off one huge tenant?

interview.q: How do you choose a shard key?
answer: It must be in almost every hot query, so each query goes to one shard.
It keeps data that is written together in one transaction on the same shard (tenant_id in B2B SaaS).
It spreads load: high cardinality and no single value with a large share of traffic; check the traffic per key before choosing.
Avoid monotonically increasing range keys (timestamps, sequential IDs) as the only key: all new writes go to one shard.
Plan for the outlier: a directory mapping lets you move one large tenant to its own shard.
followups: Hash vs range sharding: trade-offs?
How do you handle queries without the shard key?

interview.q: How would you move a large tenant to a new shard without downtime?
answer: Copy existing data to the new shard (snapshot), then stream ongoing changes (logical replication or CDC filtered by tenant).
Verify: row counts and checksums per table until the copy is in sync.
Cut over: briefly block or queue writes for that tenant, wait for the last changes, flip the directory entry, resume.
Keep the old data read-only for a while for rollback, then delete it.
This is why a directory (tenant → shard) is better than pure hashing: the move is one row change.
followups: How long can the write pause be, and how do you keep it short?
What about caches that still point to the old shard?

one: Keeping a set of open database connections and lending them to requests, instead of opening a new one each time.
an: A taxi rank. Cars wait ready; you take one and return it. Building a new car for each trip would be absurd.
how: Opening a DB connection costs several network round trips (TCP, TLS, authentication), and Postgres starts a new server process for it, which uses its own memory.
Application pools (in your DB driver/ORM) keep e.g. 10 connections per process. External poolers like PgBouncer (or a provider's pooled endpoint) sit between many app instances and the DB.
Math matters: 50 containers × 20 connections each = 1000 connections, far above the Postgres default max_connections of 100.
why: Serverless and autoscaled apps can open thousands of connections and knock the database over. Pool sizing is a frequent production incident.
trade: Transaction-mode poolers break session features (SET, session advisory locks, LISTEN, temp tables) because each transaction may run on a different server connection. Protocol-level prepared statements work through PgBouncer 1.21+ when max_prepared_statements is set (on by default since 1.24). Bigger pools are not faster beyond what the DB's CPUs and disks can serve.

myth.r: Past a point the DB thrashes on context switching and locks. Small pools with queued requests often beat huge pools.

q.s: Your serverless API spikes to 800 concurrent function instances and Postgres starts refusing connections. Fix?
o: Raise max_connections to 10,000
Put a pooler (PgBouncer / provider's pooled endpoint) between functions and the DB
Add indexes
Use a CDN
q.e: Each function instance holds its own connection. A pooler multiplexes them onto a small set of real connections.

more: Session vs transaction vs statement pooling modes
Pool size formula: roughly cores × 2 for the DB, not "as many as possible"
Connection lifetime and idle timeouts
HTTP-based drivers for serverless (Neon, Supabase, PlanetScale)
Leaked connections from unreleased clients
lab: Write a script that opens a new pg.Client per query in a loop; time 500 queries. Then use a pg.Pool; compare.
Set max_connections low in a local Postgres and run 200 concurrent requests without a pool to see the errors.
Run PgBouncer in Docker in transaction mode in front of Postgres and repeat.

plain:
Opening a database connection is slow (handshakes and login) and each open connection uses memory on the database server. A connection pool keeps a few connections open and lends them to requests, then takes them back.

The database can only handle a limited number of connections, so the pool size of every app instance adds up.
bridge: It is like reusing one fetch keep-alive connection instead of opening a new TCP connection for every request, but for your database.

walk.title: Serverless meets Postgres
steps: Your API runs as serverless functions. Each function instance opens its own DB connection.
A marketing email goes out. Traffic spikes, and the platform starts 500 function instances.
500 connections hit Postgres, which allows 100. New requests fail with “too many clients”.
You add a pooler (PgBouncer, or your provider's pooled connection URL) between the functions and Postgres.
The functions now connect to the pooler, which shares about 20 real connections among them. The spike passes without errors.

terms: An open, logged-in link between your app and the database.
A set of reusable open connections.
The database's limit on simultaneous connections.
A popular external pooler for Postgres.
insights: Your real connection count is pool size × instances at the autoscaling maximum, plus workers, cron jobs and admin tools.
A pool that waits forever hides problems. Set a checkout timeout so exhaustion becomes a visible error.
A small pool with a queue in the app usually beats a big pool: waiting in Node is cheap, waiting inside Postgres is not.

prod.summary: In production, connection limits are a shared budget: every app instance, worker, cron job, migration and admin tool takes from the same max_connections. Seniors calculate the worst case (max replicas × pool size), keep app pools small, put a pooler in front for serverless or many instances, and set timeouts so a slow database causes fast, visible errors instead of a hung app.
checklist: Worst-case connections = (max autoscaled instances × pool max) + workers + cron + admin, and it stays below max_connections minus reserved slots.
Every pooled client is released in finally; prefer pool.query() for single statements so release is automatic.
connectionTimeoutMillis is set (node-postgres default 0 = wait forever), so pool exhaustion shows up as errors, not hung requests.
Serverless functions connect through a pooler (PgBouncer, RDS Proxy, the provider's pooled URL) and create the pool outside the handler so warm invocations reuse it.
For PgBouncer in transaction mode, the code uses no session state (SET without LOCAL, session advisory locks, LISTEN).
Dashboards show active vs idle connections from pg_stat_activity, pool wait time, and the count of “idle in transaction” sessions.
Migrations and long jobs use a direct (session) connection, not the transaction pooler.
numbers: Postgres max_connections defaults to 100, with 3 reserved for superusers (superuser_reserved_connections).
node-postgres Pool defaults: max 10, idleTimeoutMillis 10,000, connectionTimeoutMillis 0 (no timeout).
PgBouncer defaults: pool_mode = session, default_pool_size = 20 per user/database pair, max_client_conn = 100.
PgBouncer added prepared statement support in transaction mode in 1.21 (2023); max_prepared_statements defaults to 200 since 1.24.
failures: Postgres logs and clients show “FATAL: sorry, too many clients already” during a traffic spike.

Autoscaling multiplied app pools past max_connections. Put a pooler in front, lower per-instance pool size, and cap max instances; raising max_connections a lot just moves the problem to memory and CPU.
Requests hang forever under load; DB CPU is low; no errors in logs.

Clients were checked out and never released (an early return or throw before release()), so the pool is empty and new requests wait with no timeout. Release in finally, set connectionTimeoutMillis, and alert on pool wait count.
After moving to PgBouncer transaction mode, a feature that uses SET search_path or advisory locks behaves randomly.

Session state set on one server connection is gone or leaks to another client on the next transaction. Use SET LOCAL inside the transaction, transaction-level advisory locks, or a session-mode pool for that feature.
Throughput drops when the pool size is raised from 20 to 200.
The DB now runs 200 active queries on 8 cores, causing lock contention and context switching. Return to a small pool; let requests queue in the app, where waiting is cheap.

code.note: With 12 instances × max: 10 = 120 connections, this already exceeds a default Postgres; that is when you add PgBouncer or lower max.

qs.s: Your Node API runs on Kubernetes with an HPA of 4–30 pods, each with pg.Pool({ max: 15 }). A cron worker uses 10 more connections. Postgres has max_connections = 200. What happens at peak?
o: Nothing; Postgres queues extra connections
Only 15 connections are used in total
Pods crash because of memory
Up to 30 × 15 + 10 = 460 connections are attempted, so new connections fail with “too many clients” once the ~197 non-reserved slots are used
qs.e: Pool limits are per process. Worst case is max replicas × pool size plus other clients. Postgres does not queue connections beyond its limit; it rejects them. Fix with a pooler or smaller pools.

qs.s: With PgBouncer in transaction mode, a migration tool fails, and a background worker using LISTEN orders_changed never receives notifications. Why?
o: PgBouncer blocks all DDL
LISTEN and session-level state need the same server connection across transactions; in transaction mode each transaction can land on a different one
PgBouncer does not support SSL
max_client_conn is too low
qs.e: Transaction pooling hands the server connection back after every transaction, so session features break. Connect migrations and LISTEN workers directly to Postgres (or through a session-mode pool).

qs.s: A handler does const c = await pool.connect(); const r = await c.query(...); if (!r.rows.length) return null; ...; c.release();. After a few hours in production, all requests time out. What is the bug?
o: The early return null skips release(), so every “not found” request leaks a connection until the pool is empty
pool.connect is deprecated
The query is missing an index
The pool max is too low
qs.e: Each leak permanently removes a connection from the pool. Once all 10 are gone, every request waits. Release in finally or use pool.query for single statements. A bigger pool only delays the outage.

qs.s: Read this PgBouncer config. 300 app connections try to connect at once during a spike. What happens?

code.title: pgbouncer.ini
code.src:
[databases]
app = host=10.0.1.5 port=5432 dbname=app

[pgbouncer]
pool_mode = transaction
max_client_conn = 100
default_pool_size = 20
reserve_pool_size = 0
query_wait_timeout = 120

o: All 300 connect; PgBouncer opens 300 server connections to Postgres
All 300 connect and share 20 server connections with no waiting
About 100 clients connect and the rest are refused; the connected clients share 20 server connections and wait in a queue when all 20 are busy
PgBouncer crashes because 300 is more than the pool size
qs.e: max_client_conn limits client connections to PgBouncer itself; the extra ones get “no more connections allowed (max_client_conn)”. default_pool_size limits real server connections per user/database pair; clients over that wait in a queue for up to query_wait_timeout. PgBouncer never opens more server connections than the pool size, which is the whole point.

qs.s: This serverless handler works in testing. In production, Postgres connections climb steadily and then fail with “too many clients”. What is the bug?

code.title: api/user.ts

o: A new pool is created on every invocation and never closed, so each warm instance keeps adding idle connections; create the pool once at module level (outside the handler) and connect through a pooler
max: 5 is too low; raise it to 50
pool.query leaks the client; it must be released manually
The query needs a LIMIT 1
qs.e: The pool lives as long as the warm function instance, but the code throws its reference away after every call, while its connections stay open until the idle timeout. Module-level pools are reused across warm invocations. pool.query does release its client automatically, so that option is a common but wrong belief.

qs.s: An API handles 2,000 requests per second. Each request runs one query that holds a connection for 5 ms on average. Roughly how many connections are busy at any moment (Little's law: busy = rate × time)?
o: About 2,000
About 10
About 400
About 100
qs.e: 2,000/s × 0.005 s = 10 connections busy on average. Add headroom for bursts and slow queries and a total of 20–40 is plenty. This is why a small pool serves a lot of traffic, and why 2,000 connections (“one per request per second”) is a misunderstanding of how pools work.

qs.s: Users report hanging pages. You run this on Postgres. What is the most likely cause, and the fix?

pid  | state               | xact_age | query
------+---------------------+----------+------------------------------------

o: The UPDATE needs an index on carts.id
Postgres has run out of max_connections
The pool is too small; raise it from 10 to 100

Code locks a cart with FOR UPDATE, then awaits something slow (like a payment API) before COMMIT; locks and pooled connections are held. Move the external call outside the transaction and set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout
qs.e: “idle in transaction” means the database finished the last statement and is waiting for the app to send the next one. The query column shows the last statement, so the app is busy elsewhere while it holds the row lock and the connection. A bigger pool would only let more requests pile up on the same locks.

interview.q: How would you size the database connection pool for a service running on Kubernetes?
answer: Start from the database's budget: max_connections minus reserved slots, shared by every service, worker, cron job, migration and admin tool.
Per pod: max pool = budget ÷ max replicas (from the HPA, not the usual count). 30 pods × 10 = 300 already exceeds a default Postgres.
Estimate need with Little's law: requests/s × average time a connection is held. Usually a small number per pod is enough.
The useful total of busy connections is limited by DB CPU cores and disk; past roughly a few times the core count, more connections add contention, not throughput.
Set connectionTimeoutMillis so pool exhaustion becomes a fast error, and alert on pool wait time.
If the math does not fit, put PgBouncer (or the provider's pooler) in front rather than raising max_connections.
followups: What metric tells you the pool is too small, as opposed to the DB being too slow?
How does this change for a background worker that runs long transactions?

interview.q: A team moves its API to serverless functions and Postgres starts failing at peak. What happened and how do you fix it?
answer: Each function instance has its own process, so each holds its own connection(s); 500 concurrent instances means about 500 connections.
Postgres creates one server process per connection, so memory and context switching grow with the count; it rejects new ones over max_connections.
Fix: connect through a pooler (PgBouncer, RDS Proxy, the provider's pooled URL) in transaction mode, and keep a tiny pool (1–2) per instance created outside the handler.
Know what transaction mode breaks: session SET, session advisory locks, LISTEN, temp tables. Migrations go through a direct connection.
Optionally cap function concurrency, or use an HTTP-based driver from the provider.
followups: Why not just raise max_connections to 5,000?
How do prepared statements behave behind PgBouncer in transaction mode?

interview.q: Explain PgBouncer's pooling modes. Which would you choose for a typical web API?
answer: Session mode: a client keeps one server connection until it disconnects. Everything works, but it saves little if clients stay connected.
Transaction mode: a server connection is lent for one transaction and then returned. Best reuse; the usual choice for web APIs and serverless.
Statement mode: returned after each statement; multi-statement transactions are not allowed. Rarely used.
Transaction mode breaks session state. Use SET LOCAL, transaction-level advisory locks (pg_advisory_xact_lock), and a direct connection for LISTEN and migrations.
Protocol-level prepared statements work in transaction mode since PgBouncer 1.21 when max_prepared_statements is above 0 (default 200 since 1.24).
followups: A feature uses SET search_path per tenant. What happens after switching to transaction mode?
Where would you run PgBouncer: as a sidecar per pod or as a central service?

videos.t: Database connection pools make every engineer go crazy.. here's why
videos.why: Why pools exhaust and how to size them.

one: Fetching a list with one query, then running one more query per item. 100 items, 101 queries.
an: Going to the shop for eggs, coming home, then going back for milk, then back again for bread. One list, one trip.
how: Classic shape: posts = getPosts(), then for post in posts: post.author where each .author triggers a query.
Fixes: a JOIN; eager loading in the ORM (include, select_related, with); or a second query with WHERE id IN (...); or DataLoader in GraphQL.
Detect it by logging query counts per request, or with APM traces showing dozens of identical short queries.
why: Each query is only 2ms locally, so it looks fine. With network latency to a managed DB (say 5ms) and 200 rows, the page takes a second.
trade: Over-eager loading (joining everything everywhere) creates its own huge, slow queries. Load what the screen needs.

myth.m: The DB is fast, so many small queries are fine.
myth.r: The cost is round trips, not query time. Latency adds up linearly.

q.s: A trace shows one request making 240 nearly identical SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ? queries. Name and fix?
o: Hot shard; reshard
N+1; batch with WHERE id IN (...) or eager-load
Replication lag; read primary
Deadlock; retry
q.e: Same query shape repeated per row is the N+1 signature.

more: Detecting it automatically in tests (query count assertions)
Batching in GraphQL vs REST
JOIN vs separate IN query trade-offs (row explosion)
Lateral joins for "top N per group"
ORM-specific eager loading APIs
lab: Build an endpoint that lists 50 orders with customer names using a loop of queries. Log the query count.
Fix with a JOIN; then fix with a second IN query; compare SQL and timings.
Write a test that fails if the endpoint runs more than 3 queries.

plain:
The N+1 problem: you run 1 query to get a list of N items, then 1 more query for each item to get related data. 50 orders = 51 queries.

Each query is fast on its own, but the waiting adds up, especially when the database is on another server.
bridge: It is the backend version of a frontend waterfall: rendering a list where each row component does its own fetch on mount. 50 rows, 50 requests.

walk.title: Spotting and fixing it
steps: Code: orders = getOrders(), then for each order, getCustomer(order.customerId).
Query log for one page load: 1 query for orders, then 50 almost identical SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id = ?.
With 4ms network time per query, that is 200ms of pure waiting.
Fix A: one JOIN query returning orders with customer names.
Fix B: collect all customer IDs and run one WHERE id IN (...) query. Either way: 1–2 queries instead of 51.

terms: One query for a list, then one per item.
Telling the ORM to load related data up front.
Combining rows from two tables in one query.
Combining many small lookups into one.
insights: Looks fine on localhost (DB is near), gets slow in production (DB is a network hop away).
The signature in traces and logs: the same query shape repeated many times in one request.
You can write a test that fails if an endpoint runs more than N queries.

prod.summary: In production, N+1 shows up as an endpoint whose latency grows with the size of the list: fine for a user with 5 orders, 3 seconds for one with 500. Seniors find it in traces (many identical spans per request), fix it with a join or one batched = ANY($1) query, and lock the fix in with a query-count test so the next refactor does not bring it back.
checklist: APM traces for list endpoints show a small, fixed number of DB spans regardless of page size.
ORM queries for lists say what to load (include/select, relationLoadStrategy, select_related/prefetch_related) instead of relying on lazy loading.
GraphQL resolvers for relations go through a per-request DataLoader.
Batched lookups use one array parameter (WHERE id = ANY($1)) instead of building IN ($1, $2, ... $n) with thousands of parameters.
Integration tests assert a maximum query count for key endpoints.
List endpoints are paginated, so even a correct batch query has a bounded size.
Eager loads are checked for row explosion: joining two one-to-many relations at once multiplies rows.
numbers: The Postgres wire protocol limits one statement to 65,535 bind parameters, so a huge IN ($1 … $n) list fails; one array parameter with = ANY($1) avoids that.
Latency math: 200 rows × 5 ms network round trip = 1 second spent only waiting, even if each query runs in 0.1 ms.
pg_stat_statements shows it clearly: a query with very high calls and tiny mean_exec_time is a typical N+1 suspect.
failures: The orders page p95 is 2.4 s for big customers but 80 ms for small ones; DB CPU is low.
Latency grows with list size: an N+1 per row (customer, address, items). The trace shows hundreds of short identical queries. Batch the related lookups or join them.
A GraphQL query for 50 posts with authors and comments sends 101+ queries.
Each resolver fetches its own relation. Add DataLoader per request so all author loads in one tick become a single WHERE id = ANY($1) query.
After “fixing N+1” with eager loading, a list endpoint returns 40 MB and takes longer than before.
Joining two one-to-many relations (items and comments) multiplies rows (row explosion), and every column is loaded. Load each relation with its own batched query and select only the needed columns.
A batched query that worked in tests fails in production with a protocol error about bind parameters when a customer has 80,000 items.
The ID list was expanded into one placeholder per ID past the 65,535 limit. Pass the IDs as one array parameter: WHERE id = ANY($1::bigint[]).

code.title: From N+1 to two queries with one array parameter
code.note: A single JOIN would also work here; the separate batched query is better when the related rows are wide or when several relations would multiply rows.

qs.s: An endpoint lists 100 posts. For each post it runs 1 query for the author and 1 for the like count. The DB is 3 ms away (round trip), queries run in under 1 ms. Roughly how much time is spent on round trips, and how many queries after batching both relations?
o: About 30 ms; 100 queries
About 600 ms; 201 queries
About 3 ms; 2 queries
About 600 ms before; 3 queries after (posts, authors by ANY, like counts grouped by post_id)
qs.e: 1 + 100 + 100 = 201 queries × 3 ms ≈ 600 ms of waiting. Batching gives 3 queries: posts, authors WHERE id = ANY(...), and SELECT post_id, count(*) ... GROUP BY post_id.

qs.s: A REST endpoint is fast in development (DB on localhost) and slow in production (managed DB in the same region). Query plans are identical and each query takes 0.3 ms. What is the most likely cause?
o: Production has fewer indexes
Many sequential queries per request; each now pays a network round trip of a few ms instead of microseconds
Production uses a different isolation level
The ORM version is different
qs.e: N+1 hides on localhost because round trips cost almost nothing there. In production the network time multiplies by the query count. Count queries per request in the trace.

qs.s: A teammate fixes an N+1 with include: { items: true, reviews: true, images: true } on a list of 50 products, using a single SQL JOIN. Each product has about 10 items, 20 reviews and 5 images. What is the risk?
o: The JOIN can return about 50 × 10 × 20 × 5 = 50,000 rows of duplicated data
None; one query is always best
The database cannot join more than two tables
Images cannot be joined
qs.e: Joining several one-to-many relations in one query produces a cartesian product per parent. Separate batched queries per relation (or JSON aggregation) return 50 + 500 + 1000 + 250 rows instead.

qs.s: This GraphQL server batches author lookups with DataLoader. Users report seeing an old display name for minutes after changing it, and in rare cases the wrong user's data. What is the bug?

code.title: loaders.ts

o: = ANY($1) does not work with string IDs
The loader is created once at module level, so its cache is shared by all requests forever; create a new DataLoader per request (in the GraphQL context)
The results are returned in the wrong order
DataLoader cannot batch inside resolvers
qs.e: DataLoader caches every key it has loaded. A global instance becomes a process-wide cache with no expiry and no per-user permissions. Per-request loaders keep the batching and limit caching to one request. The code already maps results back to the order of ids, which DataLoader requires, so the ordering option is wrong.

qs.s: A teammate “fixes” an N+1 by running the per-item queries in parallel. The pool has max: 10. A page has 200 items. What is the effect under load?

code.title: orders.ts

o: One request now takes all 10 pool connections and queues 190 more queries, so other requests wait; it is still 201 queries. Use one batched query with = ANY($1)
It is fixed: parallel queries take the time of one
Postgres runs them in a single transaction automatically
It fails because Promise.all cannot run database queries
qs.e: Parallelism hides the latency for one user in a quiet test, but the work is the same 201 round trips. Under load each page holds the whole pool, so latency grows for everyone. One WHERE order_id = ANY($1) query does the same work in one round trip.

qs.s: Read this pg_stat_statements extract from the last hour. Which query is the most likely N+1 to fix first?
o: A, because it has the highest mean time per call
C, because 1.9 s per call is the slowest
B: a tiny lookup by primary key called ~167 times per orders query; besides its DB time, each call costs an app-to-DB round trip not shown here
D, because updates are expensive
qs.e: The N+1 signature is very high calls with a tiny mean on a by-id lookup, called many times per parent query (6,880,000 ÷ 41,200 ≈ 167). Its total DB time is already the largest, and the real cost is bigger: total_ms counts only server time, not the network round trip each call pays. C is slow too, but runs 60 times.

qs.s: An endpoint passed its query-count test last month. A developer added authorName to the response DTO, and now the endpoint runs 51 queries for 50 posts. The repository code did not change. Where did the N+1 come from?
o: The database planner changed the plan
The test database has fewer rows
Pagination was removed
The serializer reads post.author.name, which the ORM loads lazily, one query per post; eager-load the relation in the repository and keep the query-count test
qs.e: Lazy loading turns any property access into a query, even in code far from the data layer, such as a serializer or a template. That is why seniors prefer explicit loading (include/select) for list endpoints and a test that counts queries. A plan change affects speed, not the number of queries.

interview.q: What is the N+1 problem, and how would you find it in a running production system?
answer: One query loads a list, then one more query runs per item for related data; cost grows with list size.
It hides locally because round trips are microseconds; in production each costs milliseconds, so 200 rows × 5 ms = 1 s of waiting.
Find it in APM traces: many identical short DB spans inside one request.
Or in pg_stat_statements: a by-id query with huge calls and tiny mean time.
Or by latency that correlates with result size (big customers slow, small ones fast) while DB CPU stays low.
Prevent regressions with query-count assertions in integration tests.
followups: How would you write that query-count test?
Can caching fix N+1?

interview.q: When do you fix an N+1 with a JOIN and when with a separate batched query?
answer: JOIN: one round trip; good for to-one relations (order → customer) and when you need to filter or sort by the related table.
Batched = ANY($1) query: good for to-many relations, because joining several one-to-many relations multiplies rows (row explosion).
Batched queries also avoid repeating wide parent columns in every joined row.
JSON aggregation (json_agg) or a LATERAL join can return nested data in one query when the shape is fixed.
Either way: select only needed columns and keep the list paginated.
followups: What does an ORM's include do under the hood for to-many relations?
How do you handle a list of 100,000 IDs?

interview.q: How does DataLoader work, and what can go wrong with it?
answer: It collects all load(id) calls made in the same tick of the event loop and calls your batch function once with all IDs.
The batch function must return results in the same order and length as the keys (null for missing), or data goes to the wrong parent.
It caches per instance, so create one per request; a global instance leaks data across users and never refreshes.
It batches per loader and per tick; nested levels still produce one query per level, which is fine (bounded), not per item.
Watch batch size: very large key lists may need chunking.
followups: How would you batch a to-many relation (posts → comments) with DataLoader?
Does DataLoader help in a REST API?

one: Systems like Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Meilisearch or Typesense built for relevance-ranked text search, typo tolerance and facets.
an: A librarian who understands that "run", "running" and "ran" are the same idea and puts the best matches first, rather than a clerk matching exact strings.
how: They build an inverted index: for each word, the list of documents containing it. Text is tokenized and normalized (lowercase, stemming, per-language analyzers; Korean and other languages need special tokenizers).
Results are ranked by relevance (BM25 and friends), with filters and facet counts ("Brand: Nike (42)").

The DB stays the source of truth; you sync data into the search index via events or periodic jobs. Vector search (embeddings in pgvector etc.) adds meaning-based matching and is often combined with keyword search (hybrid).
why: LIKE '%term%' cannot use a normal index, has no ranking, no typo tolerance, and dies at scale.
trade: Another system to keep in sync, so search results can be slightly stale. Postgres full-text search or pg_trgm is often enough before adding one.

myth.m: Search is just a WHERE clause.
myth.r: Relevance, language analysis and typo tolerance are the product. That is a different data structure from a B-tree.

q.s: Search for "iphone" must find "iPhone 15 Pro" and tolerate "iphnoe". Products: 30k rows in Postgres. Sensible first step?
o: LIKE '%iphnoe%'
Postgres full-text search plus pg_trgm, or a light engine like Meilisearch/Typesense
Shard the DB
A graph DB
q.e: At 30k rows you do not need a cluster. Trigram similarity handles typos; move to a dedicated engine when relevance tuning needs grow.

more: Analyzers and tokenizers per language (Korean needs morphological analysis, e.g. nori/mecab)
BM25 relevance scoring
Facets and filters
Hybrid search: keyword + vector, combined with reciprocal rank fusion
Keeping the index in sync (dual write vs CDC vs batch)
lab: Add Postgres full-text search to a table: a generated tsvector column, a GIN index, and a ranked query with ts_rank.
Enable pg_trgm and implement typo-tolerant search with similarity().
Run Meilisearch in Docker, index the same data, and compare typo tolerance and relevance.

plain:
Searching text well is a different job from looking up rows. Users type “iphone 15 pro max” or make typos, and expect the best matches first.

Search engines build an inverted index: for every word, a list of documents containing it. They understand word forms, tolerate typos, and rank results by relevance.
bridge: A product search box with a LIKE '%term%' query works for a demo and fails in production: slow, no typo tolerance, no “best match first”.

walk.title: Upgrading a shop's search step by step
steps: Today: WHERE name ILIKE '%iphnoe%' finds nothing and scans every row.
Step 1: Postgres full-text search with a GIN index: fast, understands words and ranking.

Step 2: add the pg_trgm extension for typo tolerance. Compare against single words (<%, word similarity) with a threshold tuned on your data: then “iphnoe” matches “iPhone”. Plain % on the whole name misses it.
Step 3: when you need facets (“Brand: Apple (42)”), synonyms and fine relevance tuning, move to a search engine like Meilisearch or Elasticsearch.
Postgres stays the source of truth; a background job keeps the search index in sync.

terms: A map from each word to the documents containing it.
Ordering results by how well they match.
Splits and normalises text into searchable words; language-specific.
Counts per category shown as filters.
insights: You can go far with Postgres full-text search before adding a search engine.
Every extra search system must be kept in sync, so results can be briefly out of date.
Korean, Japanese and Chinese need special tokenizers; default English rules split words badly.

prod.summary: In production, search is a product feature with its own data pipeline: the database stays the source of truth, and a sync process (outbox, CDC or batch) feeds the search index. Seniors care about relevance for real queries (including typos and the user's language), how stale the index can be, how to rebuild it without downtime, and keeping deep pagination and wildcard queries from hurting the cluster.
checklist: Start with Postgres full-text search + pg_trgm; move to a dedicated engine when you need facets at scale, synonyms, per-field boosting or very high query volume.
The analyzer matches the language: English stemming does not work for Korean (use nori or similar), and Postgres has no built-in Korean text search configuration.
Index sync is reliable: changes go through an outbox or CDC, with retries, and a full reindex job exists.
Reindexing uses a new index plus an alias swap, so search never shows a half-built index.
Deep pagination is limited or uses cursors (search_after), not large from offsets.
A set of real queries with expected top results is tested for relevance before and after any analyzer or ranking change.
Permissions are applied in the search query (tenant_id filter), never only after results come back.
numbers: Elasticsearch index.refresh_interval defaults to 1s: new documents become searchable about a second after indexing (shards idle for 30s skip refreshes until searched).
Elasticsearch index.max_result_window defaults to 10,000, the limit for from + size.
Meilisearch by default accepts 1 typo for words of 5+ characters and 2 typos for 9+ characters.
Postgres pg_trgm.similarity_threshold (used by the % operator) defaults to 0.3.
failures: A product was renamed an hour ago but search still shows the old name.

The sync to the search index missed an event (a dual write that failed, or a path that updates the DB directly). Feed the index from an outbox or CDC with retries, and run a periodic diff/reindex job.
Elasticsearch returns “Result window is too large, from + size must be less than or equal to: [10000]”.
The UI allows jumping to page 600. Use search_after cursors, cap pages, or narrow with filters; raising max_result_window just moves the memory cost.
Korean users say search finds nothing for “삼성전자” when the product says “삼성 전자 갤럭시”.
The default analyzer splits on spaces only, so Korean compound words do not match. Use a Korean morphological analyzer (Elasticsearch nori, or n-gram based matching) and retest with real queries.
Search cluster CPU hits 100% after a marketing change; slow logs show *phone* queries.
Leading-wildcard queries scan the whole term dictionary. Remove wildcard search from the UI, and use n-gram or edge n-gram fields for partial matching.
