code.note: websearch_to_tsquery safely parses user input (quotes, OR, minus) without syntax errors. The same trigram GIN index serves %, <% and ILIKE '%term%'. Tune the threshold on your own data: two swapped letters in a short word destroy most of its trigrams.

qs.s: A shop with 2M products uses Elasticsearch fed by dual writes (the API writes to Postgres, then to Elasticsearch). About 0.1% of products are missing or stale in search. What is the most robust fix?
o: Write to Elasticsearch first, then Postgres
Increase the refresh_interval
Feed Elasticsearch from an outbox table or CDC on Postgres with retries, plus a periodic reconciliation job
Use synchronous replication in Postgres
qs.e: Dual writes fail partially (timeouts, crashes between the two). Making Postgres the single source and driving the index from its committed changes gives at-least-once delivery. Changing the write order only changes which side gets out of sync.

qs.s: You must rebuild an Elasticsearch index with a new analyzer for 20M documents. Users must not see empty or partial results during the 2-hour rebuild. How?
o: Delete the index and recreate it at night
Build products_v2 in the background, then atomically switch an alias “products” from v1 to v2
Update the analyzer setting on the live index
Run the rebuild with refresh_interval = 1s
qs.e: The app queries an alias. You build the new index next to the old one, catch up on changes, then swap the alias in one atomic call. Analyzers on existing fields cannot be changed on a live index, and deleting first causes downtime.

qs.s: On Postgres, WHERE name ILIKE '%galaxy%' on 5M rows takes 3 s. There is a B-tree index on name. What makes it fast without adding a new system?
o: A GIN index with gin_trgm_ops on name (pg_trgm)
Add a second B-tree index on lower(name)
Increase shared_buffers
Use a hash index
qs.e: A B-tree can only use a known prefix; a leading % has none. A trigram GIN index supports LIKE/ILIKE with wildcards on both sides. lower(name) in a B-tree still needs a prefix.

qs.s: In Elasticsearch, status is mapped as text. This query returns 0 hits although many orders have status “PAID”. Why?

code.title: POST /orders/_search

o: Filters do not work inside bool queries
The index has not been refreshed
term is case-insensitive, so it should have matched
The text field was analyzed and stored as the token “paid”; term does not analyze its input, so “PAID” never matches. Map exact values like status as keyword
qs.e: text fields are for full-text search: they are tokenized and lowercased at index time. term looks for the exact token. IDs, statuses and tags should be keyword fields (often a text field with a .keyword sub-field). A missing refresh would hide only documents from the last second.

qs.s: There is a GIN index. Yet this query does a Seq Scan on 5M products. Why?

code.title: search.sql

o: The query's expression uses the 'english' configuration but the index was built on 'simple'; an expression index is used only when the query has the same expression
GIN indexes cannot be used with websearch_to_tsquery
The table needs VACUUM FULL
Full-text search always scans the table
qs.e: The planner matches the indexed expression exactly. Different configurations produce different tokens, so the index cannot answer the query. A stored generated tsvector column with one configuration avoids this mismatch. GIN supports @@ with any tsquery function.

qs.s: You add vector search next to keyword search (BM25). You combine them by adding the BM25 score and the cosine similarity. Results are dominated by keyword matches. What is the standard fix?
o: Multiply the scores instead of adding them
Use Reciprocal Rank Fusion: combine the ranks from each list (score = Σ 1/(k + rank)), which does not depend on the score scales
Drop keyword search and use vectors only
Increase the number of vector dimensions
qs.e: BM25 scores have no fixed range (they can be 15 or 40) while cosine similarity is between -1 and 1, so a raw sum is dominated by BM25. RRF uses only positions in each result list, so it needs no normalization. Multiplying has the same scale problem. Dropping keywords loses exact matches like product codes.

qs.s: A multi-tenant app asks the search engine for the top 20 results, then removes documents the user may not see. Users report pages with 3 results and facet counts that include other tenants' products. Correct fix?
o: Fetch the top 200 instead and filter in the app
Hide the facet counts
Put the tenant and permission filter inside the search query (a filter clause), so ranking, paging and facets only consider allowed documents
Create a cache of allowed IDs per user
qs.e: Filtering after the search breaks paging (fewer than 20 per page), and facets are counted before the filter, which also leaks information about other tenants. Fetching 200 just makes the gaps rarer. Filters in the query are also cached by the engine, so they are cheap.

interview.q: You have a Postgres app with a slow product search. When would you add Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, and when not?
answer: First measure what users need: typo tolerance, ranking, facets, language support, query volume.
Postgres covers a lot: tsvector + GIN with ts_rank, pg_trgm for typos and ILIKE, pgvector for semantic search.
Add an engine when you need fast facets at scale, synonyms and per-field boosting, complex relevance tuning, CJK analyzers (e.g. Korean nori), or search load that should not hit the primary.
The cost: another cluster to run, a sync pipeline, index rebuilds, and slightly stale results.
Lighter engines (Meilisearch, Typesense) are a middle step for small teams.

interview.q: How do you keep a search index in sync with the database?
answer: The database stays the source of truth; the index is a derived view that can always be rebuilt.
Avoid dual writes from the request path: one of the two writes will eventually fail.
Use a transactional outbox or CDC (e.g. Debezium on the WAL) so every committed change produces an event; consumers are idempotent (upsert by ID, use a version).
Handle deletes and ordering (an older event must not overwrite a newer document).
Run a periodic reconciliation and keep a full reindex job: build a new index and swap an alias.

How do you reindex 50M documents without downtime?

interview.q: How do you measure and improve search relevance?
answer: Collect a judged set: real queries (from logs) with the results that should rank at the top.
Track offline metrics on that set (e.g. NDCG, recall@10) for every analyzer or ranking change.
Track online signals: zero-result rate, click-through on top results, reformulation rate.
Common levers: field boosts (title > description), synonyms, typo settings, language analyzers, hybrid with vectors.
Change one thing at a time and A/B test risky changes.
